#769. Meet the people set for key role in deciding Man City fate

Manchester City have been sponsored by Etihad since May 2009

They are the five individuals at the Premier League set to play a key role in the fate of Manchester City.

The competition's board has the responsibility of recommending a punishment after the seismic news in September of the club being found guilty of breaching financial rules by an independent commission.

While that three-person commission panel will ultimately decide on a sanction, the Premier League's submission will be considered, along with the view of City of course, who maintain their innocence and have appealed.

It is not known when a sanction hearing will take place, nor what sanction the Premier League will want for what it describes as the most significant disciplinary case in its history, with a fine, points deduction, expulsion or the stripping of past titles all possible.

So who makes up the Premier League's board, and how have their recommendations over punishments been received in past disciplinary cases?

Among various roles and responsibilities, the board is the entity responsible for prosecuting breaches of Premier League rules.

It comprises the league's chair, chief executive, and three independent non-executive directors, with no club representatives included - in order to provide independence and neutrality.

Do Manchester City have any grounds to win their appeal?

How much did Man City's rule breaking cost your team?

Alison Brittain has kept a low profile since becoming the league's first female chair almost four years ago. Formerly a senior executive in the hospitality and financial services sectors, she is also chair and trustee of The King's Trust Group.

Described as "sensible" by one acquaintance, in September she spoke at a university event, revealing that she was initially sceptical about joining the Premier League because she had never worked in sport.

Two senior club executives - the former Arsenal CEO Vinai Venkatesham (now at Spurs), and ex-Aston Villa CEO Christian Purslow - told her that her skillset was what the league needed, helping to persuade her to apply.

She said: "They actually spent some time talking to me and saying 'we aren't looking for a super fan. In fact we're looking for the exact opposite - somebody who will bring a different mindset. A business mindset, governance standards, be able to reset us a little bit into a different way'â¦and so I then went through the process and ended up in the job."

Describing herself as a "lifelong Manchester United fan [who] stood in the Stretford End before it had seats, as a kid" because of her family's allegiance, Brittain is now also a Brentford supporter. In 2025, she received unanimous backing from the 20 clubs to continue for a second three-year stint.

Speaking in 2024, Brittain acknowledged the league was "not without its challenges". But she has hailed what she describes as "the most exciting competition in the world", and its global appeal, calling it an "enormous soft power asset" for the country.

She also recently said that "the whole point of running the league... is to make sure the competitive balance stays really good. Because what makes us successful is this virtuous circle of anyone could win any match any dayâ¦ there has to be jeopardy."

She added: "Someone has to care about keeping that balance, because if you ask the clubs they'd rather not have that balance because they'd like to win all the time."

When asked if that was her job, she replied: "Absolutely. That's my job."

According to Purslow, Brittain has "extremely good people skills and diplomacy in a role where keeping 20 owners more or less happy is not an easy job. She is a very down to earth, straightforward person, and that plays well."

Richard Masters has been the Premier League's chief executive since 2019

The league's chief executive since 2019, Richard Masters is a much more familiar face to football fans.

When the independent commission's 'core decision' on City was announced in September, he said it "vindicates the Premier League's decision to pursue this case", and that the league has "a key responsibilityâ¦ to ensure that the rules, approved by the clubs themselves, are upheld to protect the integrity of the competition".

He added that it was "paramount that the league remains competitive and fair for all clubs and for the fans. We take that role extremely seriously."

Masters said: "There are elements of the case that remain to be decided, including, importantly, what sanction must follow for these breaches. Now we have the commission's decision, we are committed to moving swiftly through the remainder of the process, to provide certainty for the league, our clubs and fans."

Reportedly having grown up an Aston Villa fan, in 2024 Masters assured a parliamentary committee that "the Premier League board applies the rules consistently, irrespective of the club in question".

The board is completed with three other directors:

Mai Fyfield - a former Sky executive who during her 20-year career at the company led its bidding for three Premier League TV cycles, and currently sits on the board of BBC Commercial.

Dharmash Mistry - a technology venture capitalist and entrepreneur who also has experience of working with the BBC as a former non-executive director at the corporation. Mistry is "smart and theoretical" according to one colleague. He chairs the Premier League's audit and finance committee and is its representative on the FA's board.

Matthew Ryder - a senior barrister, part-time judge and a former deputy mayor of London when he had responsibility for social mobility and social engagement. He is also a board member of the Scott Trust, which owns the Guardian newspaper, alongside other non-executive roles. Describing himself as "a longstanding and passionate football fan", he also chairs the league's legal advisory group. He told a conference last year that his membership of the Premier League board had been "deeply rewarding... it's a fascinating time to be in football."

BBC Sport has approached the board members via the Premier League, but it declined to comment.

How did Man City's 'disguised funding scheme' work?

The Manchester City case is unique in its scale, and so it is uncertain how relevant previous cases are when looking at the kind of sanctions the Premier League has recommended. But it is clear that independent commissions do not necessarily agree with the Premier League's board when it comes to clubs' potential punishments.

In 2023, the league argued for a 12-point sanction for Everton after the club breached financial rules, with a commission then settling on a 10-point punishment instead, which was reduced to six points on appeal.

In 2024, the Premier League suggested that Nottingham Forest should be docked eight points over a larger PSR overspend, but the commission again disagreed, settling on a four-point punishment.

This year the Premier League argued that an appropriate sanction for Leicester City - for an overspend in 2023-24 - was a 12-point deduction to be applied in the Championship. The independent commission instead recommended that a six-point deduction be imposed by the EFL.

There is also an alternative to contested proceedings.

Earlier this year the Premier League board reached a 'sanctions agreement' with Chelsea which resulted in a Â£10m fine and suspended transfer ban after admitting making Â£47m in secret payments to unregistered agents and third parties over transfers between 2011 and 2018.

The league said: "When considering the appropriate sanction, the board noted that the club's proactive self-reporting, admissions of breach and exceptional co-operation throughout the investigation acted as significant mitigating factors."

Who is Rui Pinto? Is he a whistleblower or hacker? The BBC finds out more about the man responsible for bringing chaos to the world of football over the last decade.

#768. Billions in revenue proves Fifa right on the World Cup – but only on things it cares about

The 2026 edition of the tournament brought in untold amounts of money to Gianni Infantino’s governing body

The total hasn’t entirely stopped rising yet, still clicking away towards a final tally. Still, Fifa has already announced that it surpassed its own lofty revenue projections for the 2026 World Cup, bringing in $15bn, significantly more than anticipated. It appears that a third of that total – $5bn – came from ticket sales and hospitality alone, per reporting from the Times.

That would mean direct income from the matchgoing fans came in five times as high in the United States, Canada and Mexico as it did at the last World Cup, in Qatar in 2022, when the total stood at $929m. While 2026’s expanded World Cup added 40 games to the schedule, the takings nevertheless went from an average of about $14.5m per match to about $48m.

Which is to say that Fifa, and by extension its all-controlling president Gianni Infantino, was right.

Wrong, mind you, about what it believes anybody with a modicum of taste would think is cool and enjoyable. Like putting Robbie Williams in everything; or cramming Madonna, and BTS, and Shakira, and Justin Bieber, and Ted Lasso, and the Muppets into a World Cup final half-time show that catered to the appetites of the lobotomized; or setting up a pre-final speech on greatness by Tom Cruise.

Wrong, too, about mandatory hydration breaks, and suspending red cards, and stretching the aforementioned, accursed half-time show to 27 minutes in violation of Fifa’s own rules.

But right about all the things Fifa cares about. Which can be neatly reduced to money.

Right that exposing ticket sales – and even parking – to dynamic pricing, driving their prices far out of reach of your average fan, would pay off. Right that it could annex the secondary ticket market and take a hefty cut of resales. Right that the PR hit of cozying up to Donald Trump – who was already deeply unpopular, especially among America’s left-leaning soccer crowd – would not be mortal and, in fact, would not even cost Fifa any money at all. That tolerating the excesses of the Trump government – the disgraceful treatment of the Iranian team, its bluster about potential ICE action around stadiums and its denial of visas to fans and journalists hoping to attend the tournament – would be worth it in order to safeguard the money gusher. (These things may all yet be investigated, among about a million other things, but Fifa’s money is made all the same.)

Right, in the end, that the World Cup is too big to fail. That the decadence and cravenness of the World Cup’s organizers will, in the end, be redeemed by the tournament itself. That the World Cup is unfuckupable.

As things stand, it looks like Infantino may very well survive the fallout of his foolhardy and utterly tone-deaf attempt to quickly and unilaterally sell a chunk of the World Cup’s commercial rights to private equity. That was a bridge too far even in the world’s most cynical sport, but the tournament’s profits appear to have consolidated his power in spite of it all. Infantino has an election to get through in March, but a great many of his ardent supporters are apparently unmoved by the scandal and stand resolutely behind him. While he can’t quite do whatever he wants, it appears he also can’t commit an act grievous enough to be dislodged from power.

As Fifa pointed out to the Athletic, the World Cup’s attendance of 6.8 million was unprecedented – the previous record, from the 1994 World Cup in the United States, was just under 3.6 million. And hat means bigger payouts for Fifa’s 211 member associations, each of which has a presidential-election vote.

This, and only this, is why there is no reforming Fifa until the money stream is somehow slowed. The real power in soccer lies with the money – everything and everyone else is just a figurehead. The sport is organized and optimized to facilitate only the flow of money. We were reminded of this same truth just last week when comments emerged of Kylian Mbappé making light of a meme involving himself and China’s former leader Mao Zedong. The Real Madrid star quickly lost several endorsement deals in China, and scurried to apologize faster than he’s ever loped after a through ball.

Infantino understands this innately and behaves accordingly. And for all his blundering behavior, for all the ugliness and moral insolvency of his grubby masterpiece, the final takeaway from the 2026 World Cup is that, actually, this is all fine. It worked. Pandering to politicians? Proof, meet pudding. The money poured in at an unprecedented flow rate, a rapids of revenue. So, you know, carry on.

And that, to use a term from these lands that have made Fifa even wealthier, sucks.

Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: U.S. Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts, which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.

#767. Championship roundup: West Ham stage dramatic comeback on Scott Parker’s opening night

West Ham recover from 3-0 down to draw 3-3 at Cardiff

Leaders Middlesbrough beaten 2-0 at Wrexham

Scott Parker’s return to West Ham had looked like beginning in painful fashion but instead featured a stunning comeback from 3-0 down. The east London club’s new head coach had watched Cardiff’s Jack Moylan score a first-half hat-trick, before a rousing response after the break ended with Max Kilman levelling the scores at 3-3 eight minutes from time.

Elsewhere in the Championship, the leaders Middlesbrough went down 2-0 at Wrexham.

Parker had been confirmed as West Ham’s head coach earlier on Wednesday, taking over from Nuno Espírito Santo, who was sacked on Tuesday. The club’s former midfielder was appointed on a two-and-a-half-year contract.

A relieved Parker said afterwards: “I came in here at nine o’clock this morning and met the players for the first time, so I didn’t have a lot of input as such. As you can imagine, it was a difficult half-time talk. I just helped them tactically and told them: ‘OK, this is the way it needs to be now.’

“Certainly out of possession, we needed to be more aggressive. There were tactical changes and substitutions, and we became more front-footed. We took a few more risks.”

Parker admitted he could have skipped the dugout and “sat in a box” with his appointment confirmed on matchday. But the new head coach – who won promotion to the Premier League with his former clubs Bournemouth, Burnley and Fulham – chose to spend the night on the touchline.

“The first half was poor in many aspects,” Parker said. “We were very passive and slow with the ball. The biggest positive is the team we saw in the second half. These boys have come off two defeats. You come to Cardiff away and you’re 3-0 down at half-time. I can only imagine what they were feeling. They showed a lot of character and that pleased me the most.”

Moylan halted the initial feelgood factor among the visiting support in the 11th minute at Cardiff City Stadium. His right-foot drive from the tip of the D left the visiting goalkeeper Mads Hermansen helpless as it sped into the top left corner. Moylan was then brought down for a penalty – the Ireland midfielder got up to spank it home to the left as Hermansen dived right in the 37th minute.

Within two minutes, Will Fish thought he had turned in a corner for Cardiff’s third – the centre-back deftly headed towards goal, but Moylan was directly behind him and claimed his hat-trick after making the final touch.

After the break, it was a completely different story. Divine Mukasa reduced the deficit in the 58th minute, finishing calmly over the stranded Nathan Trott after a fine ball over the top from Jarrod Bowen, before Arne Engels capitalised on a mix-up in the home defence to make it 3-2.

In the 82nd minute, Bowen was again the supplier, curling in an inviting cross from the right that was turned in by the centre-back Kilman to make it 3-3 from close range.

At the Racecourse, Wrexham waited until the 70th minute to break the deadlock against Middlesbrough, before George Thomason smashed a shot into the ground from just outside the area, which rocketed past a crowd of defenders and through the unsighted visiting goalkeeper Radek Vítek. Oli Rathbone then made it 2-0 in the 84th minute.

Kim Hellberg, the Middlesbrough manager, refused to blame the absence of their top scorer Will Lankshear after the Championship leaders’ 11-match unbeaten run ended, but admitted it hardly helped.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

“Every team would miss their top goalscorer,” Hellberg said. “I think it’s tough when the decision is made very late and you have planned for it. That doesn’t help … You need to find ways. Today I think it would be difficult because we weren’t sharp enough. Whoever would be on the pitch there were not so many opportunities.”

Scott Twine scored a stunning, curling free-kick to give Bristol City the lead at Ashton Gate but the promotion-chasing Wolves turned the match around with two late goals from Sean Neave to make it a 2-1 win to the visitors.

Neave, on loan from Newcastle, came off the bench to score on 82 and 89 minutes to win it for Wolves, much to the delight of their manager, César Peixoto.

“The team showed character and soul to win that game. They kept on believing right to the end and so did our supporters,” Peixoto said. “We got what we deserved in the end. We created a lot of chances from wide areas in the first half without getting on the end of them often enough.

“Sean Neave is a young guy making his first steps in professional football and those goals will do him a lot of good. He has a lot of ability, but is humble and plays for the team.”

City’s manager, Michael Skubala, said: “We fell to a sucker punch. When you get to 80 minutes ahead against a very good side you have to take something from the game.

“As a group, we have to defend better. The goals were soft from our perspective and we could have been stronger to prevent the second in particular.”

#765. India increases growth forecast for fiscal year

India's Ministry of Finance has increased its growth forecasts for the current fiscal year. But it also warned about inflation, particularly for fuel and energy, amid continued instability in the Middle East.

India's Ministry of Finance expects India's economy to grow at a pace of 7.3% in the current fiscal year based on its latest assessment of current data, it said in its October economic review.

The estimate is a slight increase on the previous forecast of 7.1%.

India's current fiscal year, known as FY27, runs from April 1, 2026 to March 31, 2027.

The report contrasted these figures with global growth predictions of nearer 3%, saying "India's growth momentum, by comparison, has held firm."

The ministry said growth in various key indicators like energy consumption, port traffic, goods and services tax (GST) collections, and car sales had accelerated in the previous quarter.

However, the ministry also warned of continued inflationary pressure and pressure on the rupee currency, as well as downside risks from the El Nino weather phonemenon that could threaten soil moisture ahead of the winter sowing season.

It said that external factors like oil prices and "global uncertainties" — seemingly a reference at least in part to the instablity in the Middle East — continued to pressure the rupee's value and pose inflationary risks.

Consumer price inflation (CPI), the wholesale price index (WPI), food cost prices and fuel and power prices were all rising month for month, albeit at very different rates.

The CPI was up 5.54% year-on-year in September, but the WPI had risen more sharply at 11.39%. Food index inflation was up by 8% in rural areas, and a slightly more modest 7.18% in urban centers.

But, as in many other countries, fuel and power costs increases were in an entirely different league, at 25.85% inflation in September 2026 comapred to the same month a year earlier, prior to the outbreak of fighting in the Middle East.

Although it has been a comparatively slow decline, the rupee has been consistently losing value against the US dollar over the past five years, threatening the country's relative purchasing power internationally. This slide has picked up pace in the last 15 months or so.

But the ministry pointed to foreign exchange reserves worth some $721 billion and said that India was "well-positioned" to weather such risks and sustain its expansionary trajectory..

#764. A rivalry that changed football

Brazil's Kaka had just won the 2007 Fifa Player of the Year award but it was an awkward on-stage moment next to him that was to go viral and provide perhaps the first glimpse of a generational rivalry.

A youthful Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo had finished second and third respectively but Brazil legend Pele mistakenly handed the latter the trophy for second place at the Zurich Opera House.

Fifa president Sepp Blatter had to intervene to ask the duo to swap the trophies, with both looking suitably unimpressed.

For the next 10 years, Messi or Ronaldo won every Ballon d'Or and Fifa award going. In fact since 2007, 20 of the 29 gongs awarded for Europe's player of the year has gone to one of them.

With approaching 2,000 career goals between them, 85 trophies for club and country and countless individual awards and records, Messi and Ronaldo will forever be remembered as two of the most decorated players in history.

It is a rivalry that has defined the last two decades of football, transcending clubs, countries and competitions to reshape how the game has been played, consumed and debated across the world.

"Two players like them, competing at that level for so many years, fighting over the Ballon d'Or and scoring that many goals... I don't think we'll see it again," Argentina World Cup winner Angel di Maria, who played with both, says in BBC Sport's new documentary Rivals: Messi v Ronaldo.

Driven by a pursuit of trophies, records and a relentless desire to be the best, the pair have pushed each other to new heights.

It is a rivalry that goes beyond the ultimate 'greatest of all time' debate they have fuelled.

"They both changed football," says Di Maria.

Watch the trailer for Rivals: Messi v Ronaldo

Ask anyone who is the greatest and agreement is hard to find.

"It has to be Ronaldo," ex-Manchester United team-mate Rio Ferdinand says.

"Messi is the best there has ever been," insists ex-Barcelona player and manager Xavi.

Ronaldo has had his say in the past, stating in 2012: "You cannot compare a Ferrari with a Porsche. It is a different engine. Some people say I am better, some people say he is. They are going to decide who is better in the moment and I think it's me."

What do the numbers tell us? If it's judged on goals or Champions League trophies, Ronaldo leads the way. If it's Ballons d'Or or total trophies, Messi shades it.

For some, Ronaldo nudged ahead when he helped Portugal lift the European Championship in 2016, but Messi has since guided Argentina to two Copa America titles and a World Cup.

"For me, Messi is the best player in history and Cristiano is the greatest goalscorer in history," says Spanish football expert Guillem Balague, who has written biographies of both players.

And Deco, who played with Ronaldo for Portugal and Messi for Barcelona, says: "They are special. They are totally different from the rest. It's not normal to be on this level all these years.

"Each year, there's a lot of players who do amazing things for a few years, but being almost 20 years is not normal."

Perhaps the beauty of the GOAT debate is that it may never be settled - and does not need to be.

"They have come to appreciate each as the co-stars of the football drama they have appeared in for the last 20 years," says Jonathan Clegg, co-author of a Ronaldo and Messi book.

The pair are seen by many as polar opposites.

The dribbler against the physical specimen. The shy genius against the arrogant ego. Pep Guardiola's Barcelona against Jose Mourinho's Real Madrid. Adidas against Nike.

But, while the narrative of their rivalry was undoubtedly built on their differences, the similarities between the two were striking - even from an early age.

Both players were raised in humble surroundings. Both left their homes at an early age to pursue their dreams - Messi to Barcelona from Argentina at 13 and Ronaldo to Lisbon from Madeira aged 12 - and both struggled with home sickness after leaving their family behind.

Wall Street Journal reporter Joshua Robinson, co-author of a Messi Ronaldo book, said: "Messi and Ronaldo are always portrayed as being so different but the things that forged them in their childhoods were incredibly similar.

"They both go to a place that says 'we will take your talent and make you even greater'. That promise feels appealing but is a huge gamble. That moment of total commitment is when they realise this isn't kid stuff any more. 'If I'm going to be the greatest of all time, this is where it begins.'"

But the biggest thing that brought the pair together was their unshakeable desire to succeed as they quickly built reputations as prodigious young talents.

"You could already see something different with Messi," said Xavi. "Not only the quality but the intensity with which he did things. There was an aggressiveness in attack that I had never seen before.

"Cristiano even gave him an extra push to be a better player."

Meanwhile in England, a teenage Ronaldo was signing for Manchester United from Sporting.

"I never met a young player so confident in knowing what he wanted," said Rene Meulensteen, who was part of the club's backroom team at the time. "The moment he came to Man United it was just a logical step of what he wanted to become - the best player in the world.

"Cristiano was a fast learner. I wanted to turn him from someone who could score a goal to a goalscorer. I made a three-minute video that just showed him scoring goals and also then the opportunities he didn't score. He embraced everything."

Fast forward to 2008 and the Champions League semi-final. Manchester United v Barcelona. Ronaldo v Messi for the first time.

"You could see already Messi was the best in La Liga and Cristiano was the best in the Premier League," said Spanish football journalist Guillem Balague. "To see those two kids on the pitch together was the sign of something to come."

Manchester United went on to win the trophy, Ronaldo lifted the Ballon d'Or and a rivalry for the ages had just begun.

Watch on BBC iPlayer from 06:00 BST on Friday, 5 June

"There is no doubt being in the same league changed everything," says Txiki Begiristain, director of football at Barcelona between 2003 and 2010.

Ronaldo's world record Â£80m move to Real Madrid in 2009 thrust the pair right into the centre of one of football's most intense club rivalries - Barcelona v Real Madrid.

And by the time Ronaldo left for Juventus in 2018, the pair had won five Ballons d'Or apiece. In the nine seasons the pair were together in Spain, Ronaldo had scored 450 goals in 438 games for Real. Messi, 471 in 476 games for Barca.

But it had become far more than just numbers. By now, it was personal - and the growth of social media meant the world was watching.

"For Cristiano it was Lionel Messi and for Lionel Messi it was Cristiano. 'I need to beat this guy'," said Begiristain.

"The Mourinho - Guardiola rivalry was like a mirror for the Ronaldo - Messi rivalry. And, as players, they knew that game-winning goals were their route to one-upmanship," added Spanish football writer Sid Lowe.

"We could watch it all on our phones. And in turn, the global exposure for the Messi - Ronaldo rivalry was now sky high, absolutely off the charts. Everything they did was must-see.

"It was on everyone's lips in the press box, newspapers and social media comments, Cristiano and Leo were hell bent on outdoing each other on the pitch. Their personal battle for supremacy was symbolised by the ongoing trophy battle between the clubs."

And what a battle it was. Messi and Barcelona undoubtedly won the La Liga honours, but the Champions League was dominated by Real Madrid and Ronaldo.

In 2012, Ronaldo inspired Real to their first La Liga title in four years but it was Messi who picked up his fourth straight Ballon d'Or award - much to his rival's disgust. He went to win four of the next five.

"There is a genuine animosity that begins to grow," says Robinson. "They didn't acknowledge each other that much, they hated comparisons.

"They could not tolerate if they were the greatest of all time, there could be another in their era, in their football league."

Deco adds: "I don't think there is something similar to what happened with Messi and Ronaldo at this moment because at the same time the two clubs, Barcelona and Madrid, were at the same level and fighting for the big trophies."

When Messi scored a 92nd-minute winner for Barcelona at Real Madrid in 2017, he removed his jersey and held it up the crowd.

"In the popular narrative, Cristiano had been the diva and Messi had been the humble servant of Barcelona, but this was the moment of Messi reasserting himself on the rivalry, saying maybe for the first time in his career 'look at me'," says Robinson.

Just a few months later, Ronaldo mimicked the celebration when he scored in the Spanish Super Cup at Barcelona.

Balague added: "If you needed proof of how much it meant to beat each other, those are the pictures."

The Messi v Ronaldo rivalry in Spain may have ended when the latter joined Juventus in 2018 - but the global, ongoing debate wasn't disappearing.

Ronaldo went on to return to Manchester United before moving to current club Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia, while Messi moved to Paris St-Germain, before signing for Inter Miami in America's Major League Soccer - where he remains now.

Having seen their impact in Spain, for the first time the players' moves were as commercially motivated as they were for football reasons.

"Brand Beckham opened the door for what was possible and these two have kicked the door off its hinges," said Rob Pilgrim, head of sport at Meta for Europe, Middle East and Africa.

Italian football expert Mina Rzouki, added: "You are not buying sporting excellence, you are buying a whole one-man economy."

The numbers are astronomical and the rivalry continued.

In 2018, Ronaldo joins Juventus and sells 520,000 shirts in the first 24 hours. In 2021, Messi moves to Paris and shifts 150,000 shirts in just seven minutes.

Manchester United welcome Ronaldo back in 2021, and United's total sales of his shirt (Â£187m) are almost double those of Messi's at PSG.

On Instagram, Ronaldo has close to 700m followers, Messi has 500m. The most-liked picture in the history of that platform is the Argentine lifting the World Cup trophy, amassing more than 75m likes.

Financially, Ronaldo comes out on top - according to official channels anyway. The Portuguese has topped the Forbes Money List as the world's highest paid athlete for a fourth consecutive time, with $300m (Â£223m) in total earnings. Messi is third on the list with $140m (Â£104m).

The rivalry between the pair is only accentuated by the fact they are on either side of the sportswear rivalry. Messi with Adidas and Ronaldo with Nike.

"They have become enormous global brands and what is amazing about them is they have to say almost nothing to become the world's biggest pitch man," said Robinson.

Brands the world over threw unparalleled amounts of money to get the superstars on board.

And who could forget the iconic image before the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, with both footballers playing chess against each other on a Louis Vuitton suitcase, to launch the designer's latest campaign.

"It is known as the picture that broke the internet. It was a commercial masterstroke," said Melanie Ropp, from social media marketing company the Goat Agency. "The timing of it before the World Cup made it globally iconic."

Robinson said: "Messi has nothing left to conquer. He has that one thing Ronaldo does not, a World Cup."

And, after following the Argentine in announcing his retirement from international football, it appears the global prize will continue to elude Ronaldo.

"Now the question is did Messi win this entire era of football?" adds Robinson.

#763. 'Star Trek' star Patrick Stewart dies age 86

The Shakespearean actor landed the role of a lifetime as "Star Trek" Captain Picard. He passed away at age 86.

For Star Trek fans, he was the legendary Captain Picard; the British actor and director Patrick Stewart, longtime member of the  Royal Shakespeare Company, died on Thursday at the age of 86 following a "brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia, according to an official statement on his social media accounts.

In Los Angeles, California, far away from the small English village of Mirfield where he was born, Stewart achieved world fame. He was 47 years old when he landed the role of a lifetime in the legendary science fiction series Star Trek: Playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in "Star Trek: The Next Generation," he stepped into the shoes of the legendary Captain James T. Kirk, played by William Shatner.

Stewart brought a calm, measured and distinctly British presence that quickly made Picard a fan favorite and a cult figure in the Star Trek universe. He returned to the role decades later in the spin-off series "Star Trek: Picard," which ended in 2023, proving the character's enduring appeal.

As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, he led the crew of the starship Enterprise, a spaceship with the sizeable mission: "To explore strange new worlds. To seek out new life and new civilizations" — and most importantly, "to boldly go where no man has gone before!"

Stewart's interest in acting was sparked in the early 1950s when a teacher asked him to recite a work by Shakespeare. His passion for Shakespeare stayed with him until the end.

His parents were far removed from the glamor of the theatrical world. His father was a highly respected officer in the British Army during World War II, but at home, he was an abusive husband, and young Patrick had to helplessly witness repeated violence against his mother. Stewart wrote about his experiences with domestic violence in The Guardian in 2009. The stage, he confessed there, seemed to him "a far safer place" than reality; he saw acting as a way to escape his home life.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Patrick began acting at the age of 12. At 16, he left school early and, thanks to a scholarship, studied acting in Bristol, England. Along the way, he worked as a journalist. In 1965, he became an official member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, and remained with the theather company from 1966 to 1982. Such was his passion for the great English playwright and lyricist that he even shared his sonnets on his Twitter account during the 2020 coronavirus pandemic.

Stewart dazzled the theater world with his own stage adaptation of Charles Dickens' 1843 tale "A Christmas Carol." He played more than 30 roles himself. After its 1987 premiere in Stewart's hometown of Mirfield, the one-man show became a critics' favorite and a long-running hit on Broadway in New York.

In the same year,  Stewart went from being a stage actor to an international TV star. Star Trek producer Robert Justman offered him the role of Captain Jean-Luc Picard, one of the main characters in a new edition of the popular TV series "Star Trek: The Next Generation."

The successful Shakespearean hesitated. Until then, he had never worked in Hollywood. But his agent encouraged him to accept the role, Stewart recalled in a 2020 interview with the German newspaper Die Welt. "You can accept the offer as a start for now. It won't be a big deal, you can't revive a series as iconic as Star Trek anyway."

But his agent was to be proven wrong: Stewart led the Starship Enterprise through its galactic adventures for seven seasons and four full-length feature films. The TV series had astronomical success on Earth in a very short time. At first, the producers were at odds as to whether Stewart's British accent could really fit the role of commander of a US starship in the 24th century, but it soon became impossible to imagine the series without the subtly diplomatic Captain Picard, who often quoted Shakespeare while at the helm. It seemed as if all the time he had spent as a Shakespearean actor had prepared him to command the Enterprise, Stewart once remarked with a wink. When the cult series ended in 1994, he had ruled out ever returning to the Enterprise's command center.

In 2010, the actor was knighted by the Queen of England. Stewart considered it the greatest honor of his career to stand alongside acting greats such as Sir Laurence Olivier and Sir Alec Guinness.

Beyond the screen, Stewart has long used his voice for social and human rights causes. In recent years, he has drawn attention to issues such as violence against women, age discrimination and the protection of children.

In a June 2020 interview, "Playboy" asked the New York resident whether he was considering retiring from acting. "Never! That would mean giving up my life," replied Stewart, who was approaching his 80th birthday at the time. He was filming the second of three seasons of "Star Trek: Picard." The series ends with a final episode in which the retired Starfleet admiral makes his last appearance. In the series, Picard retires to his family vineyard in France but is drawn back into space to confront new threats to the Federation.

This series also showcases Stewart's affection for his pit bull, Ginger. In "Star Trek: Picard," Picard also has a pit bull, a loyal four-legged companion named Number One — a deliberate reference to Stewart's real-life love of the breed. For his efforts to combat prejudice against pit bulls and to support their adoption, Stewart was honored by the US animal welfare organization ASPCA, among others.

In 2024, he published his memoir "Making it So." In it, he recounts his passion for theater and his love of Shakespeare.

Now, at the age of 86, the British actor has finally departed for another galaxy. Farewell, Patrick Stewart!

#762. Erling Haaland settles thriller for Manchester City to end RB Leipzig resistance

Feed Erling Haaland and Manchester City’s totemic No 9 will score. The problem, recently, has been a paucity of openings for him.

This was true again before Elliot Anderson crossed and Haaland slid home a priceless winner for Enzo Maresca’s disjointed unit, Rayan Cherki hitting a post late on.

The win ends City’s sequence of two defeats in three games yet the manager has major issues. He has to plug a leaky defence and drill his midfield to exert control.

And there is a shaky Gianluigi Donnarumma: City’s goalkeeper was culpable for Ridle Baku’s first equaliser for Leipzig, as he was for Nicolas Jackson’s winner in the recent defeat at Aston Villa, plus two more in the Paris Saint-Germain loss last month.

The manager said: “It’s not a concern but it’s a mistake. But in 48 hours [Saturday] we have Nottingham Forest away, we need to be focused on that and then in the international break I will look. At the moment I’m not thinking about the goalkeeping situation. Gigio knows he was not good with the first goal.”

He was honest, too, about Antonio Nusa’s second for Leipzig, the forward taking advantage of a lax rearguard. “Both goals are quite silly goals we can avoid,” Maresca said.

Still, after going down against Villa and Brighton in the Premier League, the win is a certifiable tonic ahead of the Forest trip.

City’s quest to return to victorious ways featured an XI of four changes from Saturday’s Brighton reverse. Noteworthy was Maresca’s dropping of Rúben Dias as Abdukodir Khusanov’s pace was preferred at centre-back to the captain, Haaland taking the armband.

While the 2,000-plus travelling support were stationed in a quadrant to the right of Donnarumma’s goal, the noise came from the congregation behind Maarten Vandevoordt’s where a sea of red and white bounced to the tempo of a booming drum. They could roar particularly loud when Nusa flitted across City’s D and unloaded, and what should have been a regulation save for Donnarumma became a fumble – and corner for Leipzig.

As can be with this Maresca side, control was difficult to find and administer for any prolonged passage: Phil Foden twice lost the ball when turning into traffic was no aid, the second time meaning Nusa could zigzag towards goal.

The Brighton defeat featured close to zero service for Haaland and City’s 13-goal man was again hard to find, Matheus Nunes’s loose cross, when the captain lurked, emblematic. So, too, as a sign of Leipzig’s ascendancy, was Marc Guéhi scrambling to clear danger, Nusa firing in the ball from the left, and Christoph Baumgartner having space to shoot marginally wide of Donnarumma’s left post.

“Keep the ball and shift it faster” might have been Maresca’s instruction and when this happened City fashioned the breakthrough. Cherki speared a diagonal right-left into a galloping Nico O’Reilly, whose instant cross caused Castello Lukeba to panic and turn home, via a trailing left knee.

City had forced the issue and twice went close to a second moments later. First, O’Reilly floated the ball into Leipzig’s area but Haaland’s header faltered. Then the left-back was set up by Iliman Ndiaye’s cross only for O’Reilly to miss with the same part of his anatomy.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Yet as the second half began Leipzig were staring at a fifth defeat in the fixture, having won only once in six previous meetings, all in this competition.

Intent was signalled by Nusa’s mazy run along the left, his chip causing Donnarumma to push away when he might have caught. This roused the home supporters and better followed for their team – but not Donnarumma.

Anderson’s loose ball for O’Reilly near halfway was snaffled by Leipzig, who marauded down the right before Brajan Gruda fed an overlapping Baku. Now came Donnarumma’s folly because, while the right-back’s shot was true, it was steered along a very tight angle, yet City’s No 1 allowed it to go in between him and his left post.

Here was the latest goal-costing error from the Italian – one for Maresca to ponder. Yet 1-1 was still a fair result away from the Etihad Stadium so relief emanated from those in black when Ezechiel Banzuzi’s shot hit side-netting only. Donnarumma’s wobble continued, though, as he fumbled another Baku attempt, narrowly recovering.

City were about to show character and quality: Ndiaye’s pinpoint cross from the left had Enzo Fernández arriving to head in supremely and Maresca’s team led again. Not for long. Leipzig waltzed through with ease and with Nunes out of position Nusa finished expertly from the left.

After Anderson skied over from close-range, Haaland did what makes him so lethal: score with his sole chance. “Not sure how many touches I had, but most important is that I managed to help the team to win,” the Norwegian said.

#761. Muriqi caps Fenerbahce comeback to make Liverpool pay for defensive lapses

Andoni Iraola arrived in Istanbul seeking improvement from Liverpool’s attack but departed with sudden cause for concern at the opposite end of the pitch. Fenerbahce ignited Dirk Kuyt’s interim spell with a tumultuous victory after Liverpool detonated their 100% Champions League record with several defensive lapses.

Liverpool’s second successive defeat left Iraola exasperated for entirely different reasons to Sunday’s loss to Arsenal. Blame was found only in the mirror this time around. It was so careless and so unnecessary.

The visitors led twice, through Trey Nyoni’s first senior goal and a header from substitute Alexander Isak, but Fenerbahce twice hit back quickly and snatched victory when Vedat Muriqi emerged as the strongest player from a pack of red shirts. Fenerbahce’s first goal came from a free-kick, their second from a corner and their third from a long throw-in.

“Cheap goals, messy goals,” as the Liverpool head coach put it. “We knew set pieces were one of the strengths of Fenerbahce. We have been dealing with them well, both this season and today, it has been something we have been working on since pre-season, but it cost us today. The last goal was maybe because they are strong and tall but the other two we have to control better.”

Ronald Araújo resting on the bench offers one explanation for Liverpool’s weak defensive display but does not cover every fault. The visitors enjoyed large spells of control and, despite an anonymous display from Bradley Barcola as the central striker, should never have given hope to an ageing, average Fenerbahce side packed with familiar names from the Premier League.

As expected, Turkish supporters tested the eardrums with incessant whistling whenever Liverpool took possession. They were a test for structural engineers too with their constant bouncing in the upper tier of the home end. Liverpool sought to dilute the atmosphere by controlling possession. Rio Ngumoha was prominent and N’Golo Kanté should have been booked for halting one promising run by leaping on the teenager’s back. Referee Clément Turpin was in a lenient mood with both sides.

Fenerbahce had struggled to hold up play in the Liverpool half or create a chance of note when Archie Brown exposed the visiting defence with a superb ball from left-back. The pass sailed over the struggling Kostas Tsimikas and was controlled well by Mason Greenwood, before he was pushed over by the Liverpool defender. Neither Turpin nor the video assistant referee deemed it a penalty kick.

The decibel levels cranked up and went even higher when Liverpool took the lead moments later. Ngumoha was heavily involved with a darting run and shot that was charged down into the path of Dominik Szoboszlai. Brown, under pressure from Virgil van Dijk, headed the midfielder’s cross clear but only as far as Nyoni. The young midfielder swept a low volley beyond Ederson with the aid of a slight deflection off Kojo Peprah Oppong. It was a memorable milestone in the continued rise of Nyoni; the first goal of his career at the highest level.

It was also the cue for Fenerbahce to rouse themselves. The hosts almost levelled straight from the restart when Brown’s low centre was turned against Alisson’s crossbar by Irfan Can Kahveci, who may have been ruled offside. They did not have to wait long for the equaliser. After Szoboszlai was penalised for a foul on Kanté, Greenwood’s resulting free-kick took a huge deflection off Jérémy Jacquet’s stomach and sailed past the wrongfooted Alisson. The Liverpool keeper did not hide his anger at Jacquet turning away from the free-kick and leaving a costly hole in the wall.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

The second half mirrored the first with Liverpool in control until scoring and provoking a reaction from the Turkish side. Substitutes Cody Gakpo and Isak had only been on the pitch three minutes when they combined to restore the visitors’ advantage, the Swedish striker heading past Ederson from Gakpo’s left-wing cross.

But Fenerbahce again levelled swiftly when Kanté swept in a cross following a corner and Gakpo, attempting to head clear, glanced the ball away from Alisson’s grasp to give Brown a simple tap-in at the back post. “In the stadium it was almost impossible to communicate,” Iraola admitted. “It was difficult for me to give instructions and the communication must have been difficult between Cody and Ali.”

Worse was to come for Liverpool when Birmingham-born Brown looped a cross into the heart of Liverpool’s box. Muriqi, a second-half replacement for Romelu Lukaku, managed to hold off three Liverpool players – Jacquet, Alexis Mac Allister and Nyoni – and plant a header into the bottom corner. Iraola added: “It’s so frustrating because this is a difficult place to play and we were winning twice. We need to look at how we conceded the goals.”

#760. Goalkeeper Jesús Owono experiencing ‘hardest days of my life’ after De Miguel’s death

Owono says he feels ‘huge pain’ over tragedy

Investigation into medical attention De Miguel received

The FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono said he was enduring the “hardest days of my life” after he was involved in the collision that led to the death of the Tenerife striker Jesús de Miguel.

Owono had raced out of his goal and crashed into De Miguel in added time at the end of the Spanish second division match on Monday afternoon, causing the striker to experience a cardiorespiratory arrest. De Miguel was taken to hospital in Santa Cruz de Tenerife but never regained consciousness and died on Tuesday morning.

“These are being the hardest days of my life,” Owono said in a statement published by Andorra. “I find it hard to find the words and very difficult to assimilate what has happened. I feel a huge pain, the loss of Jesús. I am thinking about him, his family and all the people who loved him.

“I know that there will be many questions to address and I will face up to whatever comes with respect. But right now, sincerely, I cannot think about anything other than Jesús and the pain that we are going through. Rest in peace, Jesús.”

Andorra’s statement said that the club remained “deeply affected” by De Miguel’s death and demanded “the greatest respect and sensibility”. The homicide division of the Spanish national police opened an investigation, which is standard procedure in Spain whenever there is a death not by natural causes. Santa Cruz de Tenerife’s chief prosecutor, José Luis Sánchez-Jáuregui, told the Spanish news agency EFE that criminal proceedings against the goalkeeper were “very unlikely”.

The investigation will focus on the events that preceded De Miguel’s death, including the attention he received after medics sprinted on to the pitch. De Miguel was treated on the field for five minutes before being taken off on a stretcher and to an ambulance that waited in the corner. Tenerife had reported that medics were able to recover a pulse in the ambulance before he was admitted to intensive care.

“We can’t say if they acted correctly or incorrectly, but we can demand that all the emergency procedures follow international standards of correct practice,” Elvira González, the president of Spain’s Association of Nurses, Emergency Medics and Caregivers, told the Associated Press. “There is contradictory information. The first thing we need to know is where and when he supposedly recovered a pulse. The first minutes are critical. You can only move a person once a pulse is restored.”

Tenerife’s majority shareholder, Rayco García, told Cadena Ser radio: “There are those who say that the impact caused his death, and that later they were able to stabilise him artificially even though it was very difficult to bring him back. I prefer to wait for the autopsy and then we can take steps. I would like to see [the results of] the investigation to know if there is something to ensure this doesn’t happen again, something that could have prevented this tragedy.”

Owono had earlier been defended by his teammate Lautaro Spatz, who wrote on social media: “I also ‌want to say a few words about my teammate, goalkeeper ‌and friend, who is deeply affected by what has happened. Those of us who know him know the kind of person he is, how much he is suffering at this moment, and that he ‌would never intentionally hurt anyone. In football, unfortunate incidents can happen, but no one could imagine that one of them might end with such tragic consequences.”

The best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s action

The Equatoguinean Football Federation expressed its support, saying that Owono, who has 47 caps for the country, was going through a situation of profound sorrow and grief. He was subsequently left out of Equatorial Guinea’s squad ⁠for their Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers this month against Zimbabwe.

Owono was sent off for the challenge and immediately walked towards the touchline, only to turn back as staff began running in the other direction. The goalkeeper deactivated his Instagram account on Tuesday after receiving abuse online, with some users commenting “murderer” on his posts. Andorra said they were offering psychological support to anyone at the club who needed it after De Miguel’s death. The Tenerife president, Felipe Miñambres, had said they would need “professional help”.

De Miguel, 30, was married and had an 18-month-old child, both of whom were in the stadium when the incident happened. Flowers have been left at the stadium by gate nine, his shirt number, and a minute’s silence was held at the Canarian government building.

De Miguel’s body laid at the Tanatorio Santa Lastenia funeral parlour in Santa Cruz before being flown to the Spanish mainland on Wednesday afternoon. Tenerife’s players and staff will fly to Madrid on a charter on Thursday morning and go from there to the village of Navahermosa in Toledo province, where De Miguel’s parents are from, for the funeral. A final homage will be held at Tenerife’s Heliodoro Rodriguez López stadium on Saturday evening.

#759. Coleman in 'hybrid role' with Republic of Ireland

Seamus Coleman is without a club since leaving Everton in the summer

Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson said it was "tempting" to include Seamus Coleman in his squad for this month's Nations League matches against Austria and Kosovo despite the defender having not played since June.

Coleman, who has been without a club since leaving Everton in the summer, will instead have what Hallgrimsson called a "hybrid role" in the squad, training with the players but having a "leadership role" alongside the coaching staff.

The 38-year-old has said in recent weeks that he is contemplating retirement but Hallgrimsson said the defender, who has 81 caps, has expressed a desire to "start playing again."

"Coleman is going to be in a hybrid role this camp and he is going to do the sessions with the players but in a leadership role, in a supportive role with us as coaches," Hallgrimsson said after announcing a 24-man squad.

"Hopefully that will get him to start playing again and that is our aim to continue to push him to play. He has expressed he wants to do that.

"It is tempting [to include him in the playing squad]. How he did after not playing much for Everton makes us believe he can always do well for the national team. We will have to wait and see."

Captain Nathan Collins has been included after he missed the Republic of Ireland's opening four League B3 matches with a calf injury.

Everton's Mark Travers replaces the injured goalkeeper Gavin Bazanu, who withdrew from the last squad in September saying it "would be wrong to participate" in the fixtures against Israel.

Evan Ferguson (ankle), Josh Cullen (knee) and Jaden Umah (thigh) remain injured and are not included.

Harvey Vale returns to the squad after he missed their previous matches, while Hibernian's Owen Elding will drop to the under-21 squad this window.

Republic of Ireland travel to face Austria in Linz before finishing their Nations League campaign with a home match against Kosovo at Aviva Stadium.

Hallgrimsson's side sit third in League B3 and have won one of their past four games.

#758. A must pick or unreliable? Tuchel's Palmer dilemma

Has Cole Palmer done enough to warrant a spot in the England squad?

Has Cole Palmer done enough to earn an England call-up for their November Nations League games against Croatia and Spain?

The 24-year-old Chelsea forward is regarded as one of the stars at Stamford Bridge, but his status with the Three Lions has been the subject of major debate, particularly since Thomas Tuchel's appointment as manager at the beginning of 2025.

Palmer's withdrawal from the most recent extended three-week camp came after his omission from their World Cup squad, prompting Tuchel to say he "misses too many opportunities to play for England".

Yet there is an argument Palmer has done enough to earn an England recall with his start to this campaign - despite Tuchel's obvious reservations.

Having scored five goals and provided three assists in all competitions, only his Chelsea team-mate Morgan Rogers has had more goal involvements during the opening months of the campaign - when looking at players he is in competition with for England.

It must be noted, though, that penalties do inflate Palmer's total more than that of some of those rivals for a Three Lions spot.

When spot-kicks are excluded, he has been outscored by all of the alternatives for England's number 10 role since the beginning of last season. He has also been outscored in open play by Rogers and Real Madrid's Jude Bellingham this season.

In addition, Manchester City's Phil Foden, who - along with Palmer - was also left out of the World Cup squad, has the same number of goal involvements (eight) this season, although half of those came against AEK Athens in the Champions League.

Nottingham Forest's Morgan Gibbs-White has also created just as many chances (2.6 per game), although they are not being converted by his team-mates.

While Gibbs-White has underperformed his expected goals this season, he has outscored Palmer since the beginning of the 2025-26 campaign and also replaced him in Tuchel's most recent squad.

Palmer compared favourably with Arsenal's Eberechi Eze, who, along with Bellingham and Rogers, was selected ahead of the Chelsea attacker for the World Cup, where England took the bronze medal after losing to Argentina in the semi-finals.

Yet Palmer has struggled to make an impact under Tuchel, making just three appearances, including two starts, without scoring or providing an assist.

Bellingham, meanwhile, was named the national team's player of the year for 2026 after scoring seven goals and providing one assist during an outstanding World Cup campaign over the summer.

In terms of Palmer's direct rivals, Bellingham leads the way with eight goals and six assists during Tuchel's nearly two years in charge, while Rogers is second with three goals and three assists.

In third is Eze, who has scored three times and had one assist under Tuchel's tenure.

But Palmer, Foden and Gibbs-White will all be eyeing Eze's spot when the squad is announced on Friday (11:00 GMT).

Palmer missed Tuchel's first camp with a hamstring injury in March 2025, but went on to play 90 minutes in Chelsea's first Premier League match after that international break.

He then featured in the June fixtures, playing in a 1-0 win away to Andorra before being an unused substitute in a friendly defeat by Senegal.

During the September, October and November international breaks that followed, Palmer was managing a recurring groin problem, which severely limited his club appearances during the early part of last season.

He last featured for England in March, coming on as a substitute in the 56th minute of a 1-1 draw with Uruguay before starting against Japan, where he lasted only 59 minutes in a 1-0 home defeat.

Palmer then withdrew from the most recent international break, with Gibbs-White replacing him, after saying he had played for Chelsea with "discomfort and pain" before the call-up.

Boss Xabi Alonso has since said the attacker was "struggling" in the 3-0 loss by Brentford before the international break.

Palmer then went on an overseas holiday during a nine-day break for Chelsea's non-international players.

He took a rehabilitation coach with him and underwent an injury-specific training plan to recover.

Returning to training with Chelsea after the period of rest, Palmer signed a new contract until 2034 at Stamford Bridge.

He then played 88 minutes and provided an assist in a 5-1 victory over Bournemouth.

He has since started all of Chelsea's subsequent matches, apart from their EFL Cup penalty shootout defeat by Liverpool last week when he was ruled out by suspension. This followed his dismissal after receiving two yellow cards in the space of nine minutes during the home league defeat by Tottenham just over a week earlier.

Saturday's 2-0 win over Manchester United was his last appearance before Tuchel picks his squad on Friday, with his penalty taking his tally to five goals and three assists in 11 matches.

Chelsea manager Alonso, said of Palmer's absences from England duty: "He's committed but he needs to be fully fit to play and when he's fully fit he will enjoy his minutes.

"We need him in that moment, [both] the club and the national team."

Tuchel has, however, expressed frustration over the player and said he "misses too many opportunities" to play for England.

If Palmer is not selected, his lack of availability will likely be a major factor in the decision.

#757. ‘In our veins’: Arsenal pushed by pain of Champions League final defeat, says Raya

‘On us to make it better this year,’ goalkeeper admits

He credits self-belief as key to making decisive saves

David Raya has said Arsenal are using the pain of losing on penalties against Paris Saint-Germain in last year’s Champions League final to “make it better this year”.

The Spain goalkeeper produced an outstanding save to help Arsenal hold off Slavia Prague on Wednesday as Mikel Arteta’s side moved up to third in the league standings with 10 points from four matches.

Arsenal will face Borussia Dortmund next at home this month before hosting Real Madrid on 9 December in a showdown that could be vital to their chances of finishing in the top two and ensuring the second leg of their first knockout tie and any that follow would be at the Emirates.

That was the case last season when Arsenal became the first team to win all eight league stage matches and made it to the final in Budapest. Raya has admitted he is haunted by that experience as PSG won back-to-back titles.

“I think it is never going to be out of the system,” he said. “It is something that is going to live with us and hopefully we can win the Champions League to get that out of us. But it has to be in our veins. It has to be on us to make it better this year.”

Raya came to Arsenal’s rescue as Slavia valiantly attempted to fight back from 2-0 down at the break. His diving stop to keep out Oskar Kubiak’s header helped to make it 10 away games in Europe without defeat. Raya, who missed out on the Yashin award for best goalkeeper at the Ballon d’Or to his Spain teammate Unai Simón, credited his self-belief as key to making extraordinary saves on a regular basis.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

“Belief is really important but hard work [is, too],” he said. “I work very hard during the week to try and help the team as much as possible on these types of nights. It is just the belief that I have in myself, and the belief the staff, the goalie coach, has in me and the team. That gives you that extra edge and motivation to keep doing it every single week, and the consistency I have been playing with throughout the years is a key factor for us.”

#755. Germany's Alexander Zverev clinches tennis No. 1 ranking

Alexander Zverev is the second German man, after Boris Becker, to clinch the No. 1 spot in tennis.

Germany's Alexander Zverev is set to become the new world No. 1 in men's tennis, capping a year in which he won two Grand Slams.

Zverev is the second German man, after Boris Becker, to clinch the top spot in the sport. Becker reached No.1 some 35 years ago.

Zverev replaces Italy's Jannik Sinner, who previously held the world's No. 1 spot.

Zverev got there by reaching the quarterfinals of the Erste Bank Open in Vienna this week.

The 29-year-old is the second-oldest first-time No. 1 ranked player after Australian John Newcombe achieved the feat at age 30 in 1974.

"(It is) very special. To have the feeling to be on the top of the world is amazing," Zverev said.

"It is different than winning a tournament or a title, but it's such a special feeling to know that the No. 1 is going to be next to your name when the new rankings come out."

Among German female tennis players, only Steffi Graf and Angelique Kerber have achieved this in the WTA rankings.

Zverev's career had long been defined by getting close to Grand Slam titles but never quite reaching the pinnacle, facing stiff competition from Sinner and Spanish talent Carlos Alcaraz.

But he finally had its broke through this year, when he won the Grand Slam at both the French and US Opens.

Known for his consistency, he was just the ninth man to reach at least the semifinals at all four majors in the same season.

The Hamburg-born Zverev also won a gold medal in the 2021 Olympics.

#752. The oracle of the second quadrant

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Chao Liu has driven up and down the US East Coast — from Florida to Massachusetts — before detouring to France. His latest stop is at IFREMER, where he will continue to pretend to be a real scientist until someone finally catches on.

The machine sat between the deep-fryer truck and a three-legged goat, housed inside a canvas tent that smelled heavily of kerosene and stale popcorn. It was a massive, rivet-popped iron boiler known officially as the Differential Analytical Oscillator, although the hand-painted sign out front simply read: THE DAO BOILER — KNOWS ALL, TELLS ALL. FIVE CENTS.

By late afternoon, the fairground was a soup of churned mud and diesel exhaust.

“It don’t do lottery numbers,” the operator said, not looking up from the greasy carburettor he was scraping with a butter knife. He was a small, sour man named Silas, wearing a leather apron stiff with soot. “And if you’re gonna ask if your brother’s a bastard, save your nickel. The answer is always yes.”

Jerry shifted his boots in the sawdust. He was 19, wore a stained canvas jacket, and had spent the past three days trying to look tragically heartbroken on his front porch. “I don’t care about the lottery. I want to know about Clara.”

Silas sighed, spitting a dark stream of tobacco juice into a bucket of scrap iron. “The butcher’s girl? She left on the 4.10 rail to Lowmarsh. What’s to know? She wanted indoor plumbing and a man who didn’t smell like fertilizer.”

“No,” Jerry said, his jaw tightening as he dropped a heavy brass nickel onto the tool chest. “She said it wasn’t that. She said there was a … a fundamental misalignment in our vectors. I want to know what that means. I want the real, exact reason.”

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Silas looked at the coin, then at Jerry’s face. He let out a dry, rattling chuckle. “The exact reason? All right, kid. But the tub don’t do poetry. You want the low-voltage ribbon or the full squeeze?”

“Give me the whole thing,” Jerry said, crossing his arms. “Don’t spare the details.”

Silas shrugged, picking up a heavy, lead-lined copper helmet attached to the boiler by a thick bundle of rubber-coated cables. It looked like an old diving apparatus, dripping with mineral oil. “Put it on. Full throttle means you get the absolute breakdown. Don’t say I didn’t warn you.”

Jerry lifted the helmet. It was incredibly heavy, cold against his ears. He lowered it over his head, plunging himself into absolute darkness.

For three seconds, there was only the smell of hot grease and the rhythmic thump-thump-thump of the internal pistons. Then, the engine engaged the clutch.

The Universe didn’t open up with grand spiritual enlightenment. It opened with a relentless, deafening avalanche of raw data.

Jerry didn’t see Clara’s face, or a vision of her on the train. Instead, a cold, mechanical voice began reading a molecular ledger directly into his auditory cortex. It informed him that on Tuesday at 3.14 p.m., the atmospheric humidity had caused a 0.04% swelling in the leather of Clara’s left boot, which altered her gait by three millimetres. This structural variance, combined with the gravitational pull of a passing manure spreader, had shifted her centre of gravity exactly enough to cause a microscopic tear in the cotton fibre of her socks.

The machine kept going. It explained that the chemical composition of Jerry’s afternoon sweat contained an excess of sulfur molecules that reacted poorly with the zinc coating on his porch railing, creating a localized scent profile that her olfactory nerves categorized under Sub-Class 4: Decaying Organic Matter. It gave him the exact thermodynamic equation of the breeze that had carried the smell to her nose. It gave him the precise atomic mass of the dust particle she choked on when she tried to say goodbye.

It went on for what felt like an eternity, resolving her ‘broken heart’ into a massive, agonizingly boring list of friction coefficients, cellular degeneration rates and barometric pressure shifts. There was no love. There was no betrayal. There was only a three-hour maths problem about why a girl walked towards a train station.

The helmet was violently yanked off his head.

Jerry stumbled backwards, blinking against the harsh light of the tent. The machine was smoking, its violet glow dying back into a dull, rusted grey. Silas was standing over him, holding the helmet, looking thoroughly bored.

#747. Britain's Stojsavljevic beaten in Hong Kong a day after landmark win

Mika Stojsavljevic, 17, had shocked former Australian Open champion Sofia Kenin on Wednesday after being restored to tournament as lucky loser; Brit now inside the world's top 400; Hong Kong Open runs until Sunday, live on Sky Sports

British teenager Mika Stojsavljevic was unable to back up her maiden WTA Tour win as she was knocked out in the last 16 of the Hong Kong Open.

Stojsavljevic, 17, shocked former Australian Open champion Sofia Kenin on Wednesday after being restored to the tournament as a lucky loser with only an hour's notice.

The Londoner was beaten 7-6 (7-5) 6-4 by Turkish world No 67 Zeynep Sonmez on Thursday in a little over two hours.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Stojsavljevic entered the Hong Kong Open ranked 411th in the world but is now just outside the top 350 in the live rankings following her victory over Kenin.

In 2024, she became the first Brit in 15 years to win the US Open girls' title, following Heather Watson's triumph back in 2009.

Stojsavljevic made her Billie Jean King Cup debut for Great Britain against Australia in Melbourne in April, defeating current world No 36 Talia Gibson in straight sets.

Sonmez's reward for defeating Stojsavljevic is a quarter-final against Katie Boulter's conqueror Claire Liu.

Three-time Grand Slam quarter-finalist, Sorana Cîrstea, is the top seed in Hong Kong, with Alexandra Eala the second seed.

Watch WTA and ATP Tour tennis live on Sky Sports and stream contract-free on NOW. The Hong Kong Open runs until Sunday, with the WTA Finals at Indian Wells starting the same day.
