#745. Has a footballer ever run a marathon faster than James Milner? | The Knowledge

Plus: managers sacked after signing new deals, war victims commemorated on kits and the first club website (part II)

Mail us with all of your questions and answers

It came as no surprise to the Knowledge that James Milner had spent the early months of his retirement training for – and then running in – the New York City Marathon. Yes, the bleep test-loving former Brighton, Liverpool and Manchester City player recorded an excellent time of 3hr 9min 4sec, an average of 7min 13sec per mile. Not bad for a 40-year-old whose physique is more like that of a wrestler than a whippet. “A few years ago, I feel like I could have definitely done sub-3:00,” he said, lamenting his late-career injuries for hindering him.

In 2012 we ran a column listing footballers’ fastest marathon times, with the former Leicester playmaker Muzzy Izzet leading the pack on 3hr 22min 36sec at the 2011 London Marathon. That very respectable time has now been surpassed by the Premier League’s record appearance maker, so we thought we had better take a gulp of our isotonic energy drink and run through a few more tales of football’s marathon men and women.

More recent marathon attempts by either active or former footballers puts Izzet down in 12th place, just behind André Schürrle, who clocked 3hr 21min 25sec in Berlin last year, though clearly wanted a greater challenge than a mere 26.2 miles. This year, the 35-year-old completed the 167.7-mile six-stage Marathon des Sables in 51hr 41min 16sec, placing 675th overall. He also climbed Mont Blanc. But back to marathons, where the fastest time we can find for a female footballer is 3hr 40min 30sec by the former USA midfielder Lauren Holiday. She is closely followed by her good friends from the USWNT, Leslie Osborne (3hr 41min 33sec) and Abby Wambach (3hr 44min 25sec).

The Fulham manager, Álvaro Arbeloa, is 11th on our overall list (3hr 15min 21sec, Valencia 2019), with Kevin Kilbane, who always looked like he had a marathon runner’s spring in his step, 10th on 3hr 14min 44sec (London, 2013). A tip of the hat now to Danny Mills, father to the GB Olympic runner George Mills, with Mills Sr running the 2023 London Marathon in 3hr 12min 18sec at 45 years of age. Meanwhile, Milner’s run places him eighth as we approach some of football’s more serious runners.

The former Dundee United and West Ham defender Christian Dailly clocked a seriously impressive 3hr 6min 26sec at the 2013 London Marathon. “In 1990, I went from boys’ football in May to my Dundee United debut in August,” said Dailly after the race. “We’d be down at the beach, and all of a sudden, I’d be running through the sea at St Andrews or up and down the sand dunes. When I got to pre-season at Dundee United, I was flying, running away from everyone.” Dailly went into athletics coaching when his football career ended. We did not expect a goalkeepeer to be jostling for position towards the front of the pack, but the former Derby County and Sheffield Wednesday stopper Lee Grant hared around London in 3hr 0min 33sec this year.

And so we get to the hallowed ground of a sub-three hour marathon and a select group of only five. The Real Madrid legend Raúl González was clearly being cheered from the rafters as he ran his home marathon in 2hr 59min 22sec in 2019. “It was only the second marathon of my life. I wanted to break three hours, and I’m very happy with what I’ve accomplished,” he said. The Oxford United manager, Aaron Ramsey, used his relative youth at 35 to tear up the Stockholm Marathon this summer in exactly 2hr 59min. Arjen Robben was known for his blistering pace over short distances in his glittering career but he showed that he could blend speed with stamina as he raced round Rotterdam in 2023 in a time of 2hr 58min 33sec.

Before setting out on his managerial career, Luis Enrique trained like a demon for the Florence Marathon, with his hard work paying off as he came home in 2hr 58min 8sec. He has since continued his fitness regime, competing in the Frankfurt Ironman event and the Marathon des Sables.

But the gold medal for the fastest former footballer to run a marathon goes to Alexei Smertin. The former Chelsea and Russia utility man took endurance running seriously when he retired in 2008 and hit a peak of 2hr 48min 17sec at the Kazan Marathon in 2020, aged 45. That is an incredible pace of 6min 25sec per mile. He has since tried switching to longer distances as he has aged but believes he may still have one or two quick marathons left in him. “I’ve been leaning toward ultras. One reason is that speed declines with age,” he said recently. “I thought I’d never be able to improve my personal best [2:48:17] … [but] I have a few more years to improve my speed.”

“What is the soonest a manager has been sacked after signing a contract extension?” asks Dave Smythe.

Adam Clark comes in hot with the first suggestion: “Leam Richardson, then of Wigan Athletic, signed a three-year contract extension on 25 October 2022 and was sacked 16 days later on 10 November 2022. Wigan then recruited Kolo Touré on a three-and-a-half year contract, who subsequently lasted just nine games.”

“I’m pretty sure when Watford sacked Glenn Roeder in 1996 he’d signed a contract extension about a fortnight earlier?” suggests Daz Pearce. Good shout, Daz: Watford were not yet in their era of sacking a manager every month, but Roeder – initially appointed at Vicarage Road in 1993 – was given the boot by Watford just 10 days after signing a new one-year contract extension in February 1996. “I am sure I have learned from this experience,” said Roeder, who announced his intention to stay in the game. He would not get another managerial job for another five years, enjoying a successful stint at West Ham from 2001-03.

Not a contract extension but Kevin Cullis’s appointment at Swansea City in 1996 lasted just seven days. Cullis, who never played professionally, had only ever previously coached non-league Crawley Town’s youth team and was later jailed for fraud in 2003, and didn’t get off to the best start in Wales with Swans players reportedly ignoring his tactics at half-time against Blackpool during just his second game in charge. Cullis resigned shortly afterwards.

Elsewhere, Dave Bassett lasted less than four days at Crystal Palace in 1984, Marcelo Bielsa resigned as manager of Lazio after just two days in the job in 2016 and Leroy Rosenior’s 10-minute stint at Torquay United is Knowledge folklore. You can read more about that here.

We have received some new responses to last week’s Knowledge archive, which features some 2016 answers to the question: who were the first football club to have an official website?

“Last week, Martyn Amos reported an Ipswich fan website started in 1990,” wrote a sceptical Alan Terlep (and others), “but history records that the first known website went online in August 1991, so if that’s correct he has a claim to fame well beyond the Knowledge. A fan site that was already active in 1993 may well be the oldest or there though.”

Fellow reader Mark Francome, who works at a global IT service provider so should know a thing or two about this, emails that “Luton Town fans had ‘WHOSH’ (‘Worldwide Hatters On The Super Highway’), which dates from 1994,” while “Millwall also had ‘You’ll Never Make The Station’ from around the same time. No records exist to confirm the internet rumour that Millwall admins hacked their Luton counterparts and ripped up the HTML.”

“Portsmouth’s new kit has names of fallen soldiers on it. Are there other examples of clubs recognising war victims on their kit?” asked Simon Cook in August 2014.

Andrew Walker points us towards Raith Rovers’ away kit for the 2014-15 season, which has been designed to pay tribute to the 16th Royal Scots regiment, a battalion formed of sportsmen, seven of whom came from the Kirkcaldy club. Three Rovers players – Jimmy Todd, Jimmy Scott and George McLay – were killed during the conflict.

“We wanted to do something completely different for next season in terms of kit colours,” the Raith chair, Turnbull Hutton, told the Dundee Courier,” but at the same time the board has been considering a suitable way to mark this centenary in an appropriate manner, so we have brought these two ambitions together with our new green and black strip. “We hope that it captures the imagination of the Scottish footballing public and, through next season’s sports pages, that it ensures that we really do remember the sacrifices of our players and so many others 100 years ago.”

And in Wales, Aberystwyth Town are also commemorating the 100th anniversary of the outbreak of the first world war. “We’re the kit suppliers to Aberystwyth Town Football Club in the Welsh Premier League,” write the good folk at RM Teamwear, “and this season we produced their home strip honouring the centenary of the first world war, more specifically on the sleeves we have the names of players who played for the club and lost their lives in the Great War. Their name, rank and regiment are on players 1-14 in the war veteran player’s position he used to play. Others have “In Memory of Players of This Club Who Fell in the Great War” as seen in the attached photo.”

“Not only were Rangers v Dundee United and Manchester City v Barnsley in 2004-05 the only British league matches to finish 7-1 that season, the same opposing goalkeepers also played in both matches,” flags Stephen Toal. “Ronald Waterreus played for Rangers and Manchester City while Nick Colgan turned out for both Dundee United and Barnsley. Are there any other examples of opposing goalkeepers coming up against each other twice in the same season for a different set of opposing teams?”

“Following Coventry City’s 3-1 victory over Sunderland, I noticed a potentially unique statistic involving Luke O’Nien, who has now played in defeats against Coventry in all four divisions of English league football. Is this a first?” ponders Kirk Savage.

“Has ever been a headed goal awarded goal of the season?” wonders Rupert Sheard. “I can think of a few belters, but awards tend to go to ones kicked in.”

“Which club team has had the most international captains playing together at one time?” asks MH Zahid. “Conversely, which international team has had the most club captains in its starting lineup at one time?”

#743. Alcaraz into Paris Masters quarter-finals after Berrettini withdraws

Carlos Alcaraz has been handed a free passage through to the quarter-finals of the Paris Masters following the withdrawal of Matteo Berrettini; watch the ATP Paris Masters live on Sky Sports this week, with the WTA Finals in Indian Wells starting on Sunday

Carlos Alcaraz made it through to the quarter-finals at the Rolex Paris Masters without taking to the court after his scheduled opponent Matteo Berrettini withdrew from their third-round match.

The pair had been due to play on Thursday evening in the French capital but Berrettini has suffered another injury setback, pulling out due to pain in his arm.

Alcaraz, who is chasing his fifth tour-level trophy of the season in the French capital, will face home favourite Arthur Fils or Taylor Fritz in the last eight at the ATP Masters 1000 event.

The Spaniard will be bidding to reach the semi-finals on the indoor hard courts of Paris for the first time in six appearances.

An official social media announcement from the tournament read: "Matteo Berrettini has to withdraw from the Rolex Paris Masters. Wishing you a speedy recovery Matteo. Carlos Alcaraz is qualified for the quarter-finals."

Berrettini posted his statement of his own in Italian on Instagram stories, which translated as: "Hi all, unfortunately the pain in my arm that I've had for a few days won't allow me to take the court tonight.

"In the next few days I will have all the necessary tests to better understand what this is. Thank you all for the support and affection you show me every day on and off the court. Mat."

Fils, who will take on Fritz in the night session, became the first French player to qualify for the ATP Finals since Gael Monfils in 2016 earlier this week.

Fritz is currently 11th in the Race To Turin and still has a chance to qualify, although the American knows he must defeat both Fils and Alcaraz to reach the semi-finals to keep his hopes alive.

Alcaraz holds a 39-5 record for the season so far and has already qualified for the ATP Finals in Turin later this month having won four titles this year - Australian Open, Qatar Open, Japan Open and last week's Vienna Open.

Stream tennis with no contract on NOW and the Sky Sports App. You can watch the ATP Paris Masters live on Sky Sports this week with the WTA Finals in Indian Wells starting on Sunday.

#742. The dachshund, a humorous icon with political symbolism

From Picasso to Andy Warhol, a surprising number of artists have portrayed the German breed. But the dachshund has also at times been co-opted as a political symbol.

Pablo Picasso was renowned for having numerous muses — mostly women with whom he also had harmful relationships. But there's at least one of these muses who was freed from toxic romantic entanglement: a cute dachshund called Lump.

Before becoming his most famous canine model, Lump originally belonged to US photojournalist David Douglas Duncan.

The dog and the photographer visited Picasso at his villa in Cannes in 1967. According to Duncan, upon their first encounter, Lump jumped right onto Picasso's lap. He apparently "decided" to stay with the painter, and they lived together for six years.

The story does not reveal how Lump's decision was communicated, but that immediate special bound was immortalized through art: Picasso painted the dachshund's portrait directly onto a ceramic dinner plate that day, and Duncan did a series of photos documenting them together while the work was created.

The plate and the photos are on show at the new exhibition "The Dachshund. An Icon off the Leash" held at the Kunsthalle Bremen until March 28, 2027.

Lump also appears in many of Picasso's series of paintings reinterpreting Diego Velazquez's masterwork "Las Meninas," in which the original work's large mastiff was replaced with Picasso's adoptive pet.

With their long ears and extreme length compared to their short legs, dachshunds have a silhouette that's instantly recognizable: "It's really a dog with an iconic shape, and that makes them interesting for many things" — from art to advertisement, says exhibition curator and art historian Annett Reckert.

Alongside Picasso, a surprising number of important artists, including Andy Warhol, Otto Dix, David Hockney, Max Liebermann and Rosemarie Trockel, have paid tribute to the dachshund. "It's striking how often the dachshund has served as a muse, model and studio accomplice for them," Reckert tells DW.

Combined with this prolific artistic career, the dachshund can equally be explored from a historical perspective, since "there's also the fact that we associate them with something German," the curator adds.

Bred to track and chase badgers, foxes, rabbits and other burrowing animals, the dachshund originated in Germany over 300 years ago. Breed standards were established in 1879, and the German Teckel Club (DTK) — one of the oldest dog breeding organizations in Germany — was founded in 1888.

The name combines the German words "Dachs" (badger) and "Hund" (dog), literally translating to "badger dog." But Germans more commonly call them Dackel or Teckel.

Because of their long, narrow build, dachshunds are also colloquially known in English-speaking countries as wiener dogs or sausage dogs.

Beyond their role as hunting dogs, dachshunds have a surprisingly rich place in German cultural history, from bourgeois stereotype to Olympic icon.

Germany's last emperor, Kaiser Wilhelm II, was an avid dachshund enthusiast and owned several of them.

Two of his dogs, Wadl and Hexlsome, made history by causing a minor diplomatic incident during a visit to the estate of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, Konopiste Castle, in 1908. The dachshunds reportedly killed one of the archduke's prized golden pheasants. The attack was widely commented on in aristocratic circles, and Kaiser Wilhelm II was forced to issue a formal apology.

The pheasant incident was obviously not as consequential as another event involving Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne: his assassination in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914, which became the primary catalyst of World War I.

Still, the dachshund remained present throughout this global conflict. In propaganda maps and political cartoons, Germany was represented as a dachshund, the British as a bulldog and the French, a poodle.

The popularity of the dachshund in the United States plummeted during the World War I because of this association; those who owned one called their dogs "liberty hounds" instead of using the German word.

During World War II, dachshunds were used for military tasks such as mine detection.

However, their missions weren't as outlandish as the stories published by the UK's tabloid press relatively recently, which claimed that the Nazis aimed to build armies of talking dachshunds. The rumors followed the publication of a non-fiction book on dogs published in 2011, "Amazing Dogs: A Cabinet of Canine Curiosities," which outlined Nazi research into dogs' — including dachshunds' — intelligence and personalities.

The dachshund definitely didn't fit into the Nazis' aesthetics: "They were used in the war, too, but not in the same way as other dogs. After all, they weren't the kind of dog a Nazi would have wanted to be seen with for the sake of appearances," notes Reckert. "Take Hitler, for instance: He famously made public appearances with his German Shepherd, Blondie. They would rather be seen with a Doberman or dogs that looked big and dangerous."

The endearing potential of the dachshund is actually one of the ideas that guided Reckert in her curation of the exhibition. They "simply give the impression that they have a sense of humor," the art historian says. "That's an attribution, of course. But they really do spread good cheer and have a truly likable character."

In the 1970s, this slightly absurd and cheerful domestic companion inspired a figure embodying a new image for West Germany: the official mascot for the 1972 Summer Olympics in Munich, Waldi.

A stark contrast to the heavy symbols that represented Germany during the Third Reich — the eagle, Germania, forests, Wagner and Prussian discipline — the mascot created by renowned graphic designer Otl Aicher and his intern, Elena Schwaiger, was as iconic as the shape of the dachshund.

The designer was vehemently against including brown or any of Germany's national colors — red, black and gold — in the brand identity. Instead, he went for delicate pastel shades: "The approach to color was truly visionary," notes Reckert. "Their intention was something we are still working on today — something we still haven't completely achieved: an open, cheerful, democratic and colorful Germany."

Still today, right-wing extremist groups attempt to co-opt the dachshund as a subtle nationalist fashion symbol that appears on ties or socks, inspired by accessories worn by Alexander Gauland. On the other hand, "Dachshunds Against the Right" has also emerged as a counter-protest movement.

But altogether, Reckert has focused on the dachshund as a symbol of friendliness and joy while conceiving "The Dachshund. An Icon off the Leash." The exhibition includes halls that are open to small dogs and even features artworks and performances specifically designed for them.

The feedback Reckert's been getting in the run-up to the show also aligns with this cheerful image. She notes that hardly a day goes by without something arriving in the mail related to the dachshund — whether pictures, artworks or information about dachshund-related events.

"It's really crazy," she says, showing examples of the stuff she's received. "I've never had an exhibition that was greeted ahead of its opening in such a friendly, diverse way. It's almost a bit uncanny, really."

#741. ‘She can do what Beckham did’: Océane Hurtré making waves at Birmingham

WSL’s second-highest goalscorer is likened to England legend for her crossing and has earned France call-up

At the conclusion of Birmingham’s warm-up, the players quietly and carefully placed their footballs into a draw-string bag. All except one, Océane Hurtré, who nonchalantly chipped hers straight into the bag from about 15 yards. It was an innocuous moment that might have escaped most onlookers at Hednesford Town’s Keys Park but it demonstrated the swagger with which she is playing.

To observe the 22-year-old warming up before the 1-1 League Cup draw at Aston Villa last week was to witness a player making skills look easy, taking one touch where others took two and pulling off no-look passes. She is backing up that panache in the Women’s Super League, as the joint second-highest goalscorer with six from the promoted side’s opening eight matches. Only Khadija Shaw has scored more.

Add in two WSL assists and a goal and an assist on her France debut last month and it has been a breakthrough campaign for Hurtré that very few expected, except perhaps those who followed closely her career in France. They include the former France head coach Olivier Echouafni, who gave a 16-year-old Hurtré her professional debut for Paris Saint-Germain during the title-winning 2020-21 campaign, the only time a side have stopped OL Lyonnes from finishing top in the past 20 years.

“She listens to everything the coach says, she’s very attentive, she’s very focused,” Echouafni says. “She’s like a sun, because when you speak with her there’s a big light. She was always quite skilful, moving the ball quickly to draw out her opponent, and had a good shot and delivered quality crosses.

“Back then, she lacked athletic stamina, the ability to sustain repeated bursts and sometimes also struggled in one-on-one situations because she was so young, but she has made great progress since then. She has also made great progress mentally – her move to Birmingham has done her a world of good.”

WSL fans are enjoying Hurtré’s pace, skill and general attacking threats, but imprinted in Echouafni’s memory are her defensive efforts as a youngster. He recalls Hurtré, on her second league appearance, against Paris FC in May 2021, replacing the Canada full-back Ashley Lawrence with two minutes remaining. “She cleared the ball off the goalline and prevented the equaliser,” he says. “It was a very important action because, one week later, PSG won the championship.”

To describe her as surrounded by experienced professionals at PSG would be a big understatement. When she had made her debut, in Europe against the Polish side Gornik Leczna, she was on the same team as a 42-year-old Formiga. Her gratitude to PSG is clear: she was spotted at the Joie Stadium last week watching Manchester City take on PSG in the Women’s Champions League, sitting just above her former club’s bench. PSG loaned Hurtré to Dijon in 2022 to gain more first-team experience and to Bordeaux in 2023-24. An injury at each affected her game time but she left a strong impression.

“I wanted to sign Océane for two main reasons,” says Sylvain Carric, Dijon women’s general manager from 2022 until 2026, who now runs the Strasbourg women’s teams. “The first was, naturally, the quality of her left foot – it’s magnificent; she can put the ball exactly where she wants it. The second was her versatility. She’s capable of playing as a left-back, a winger or a No 8.

“Océane left a fantastic impression during her time at Dijon. She had the intelligence to come to Dijon to grow, rather than remaining on the bench at PSG. She was a very good player and an excellent teammate, always smiling. She has been supported by a very good inner circle, especially her father, who I believe played an important role in her success. As for her potential, it was obvious, especially given that left foot, but she just needed to adapt her physique for the elite level. Now that she’s brought all those elements together, I’m certainly not surprised.”

Hurtré took a risk when she joined second-tier Birmingham in the summer of 2025 but it has paid off after she helped them to win promotion and she has goals against clubs including Arsenal, Brighton and Manchester City.

Birmingham’s head coach, Amy Merricks, said last month: “We’re incredibly proud of her. I’m not going to share it but, if I did share where she was when she first came in, people wouldn’t quite believe the turnaround. There were so many areas that she needed support with, transitioning to a different country at a young age. She’s learned English, which is a massive step.

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

“Everyone sees her work on the pitch but we are fortunate to see the amount of work she’s done of it, and it absolutely translates. She’s diligent, she’s a student of the game, and she thoroughly deserved the call-up [for France].”

Hurtré was rewarded for her strong start with the WSL player of the month award for September. Sylvain Jamet, a women’s football writer for the French magazine footofeminin, saw her play at the Under-20 Women’s World Cup in Costa Rica and believes Hurtré has become “a lot faster” at Birmingham.

“Her technical ability and her set-piece deliveries with her left foot stood out,” Jamet says of Hurtré’s six years representing France’s youth teams. “Since she’s arrived in the UK, they must have worked on her speed.”

Hurtré’s goal contributions in France’s 9-0 win against Latvia have boosted her hopes of a place at the World Cup next summer. Jamet, comparing her to Chelsea’s left-sided France player Sandy Baltimore, says: “They’re competing for the same place with France now. She’s less explosive than Sandy, but she’s better technically for the crosses and passing. Baltimore’s obviously fantastic, more like a one-v-one player, taking on defenders.

“Hurtré can cross from anywhere, she can do what [David] Beckham did, basically, crossing from deep, crossing from anywhere. She had very good first cap for France. There’s a good chance she will be in the squad for the World Cup. I really expect her to get one of those 26 places.”

#739. Trophies, tears, records and rows - Ronaldo's Portugal career will divide opinion

Cristiano Ronaldo has retired from international duty with Portugal; the 41-year-old earned 234 caps, scoring 146 goals; he won Euro 2016 and two Nations League titles for his country; it comes after a falling out with head coach Jorge Jesus in the last international break

Senior Football Journalist @psmithXI

Trophies, tears, records and rows, Cristiano Ronaldo's international career had it all.

For 23 years he passionately wore the Portugal shirt. The debates about his achievements and legacy representing his country will go on for even longer.

They will primarily focus on two questions. In his pomp, should he have lifted Portugal to greater heights? And in his final years, did he hold the team back from their full potential?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

What shouldn't be lost in the analysis - when Ronaldo's record will inevitably be weighed up against that of his great rival (and World Cup winner) Lionel Messi - is that across his unmatched 234 caps, Ronaldo's brilliance helped deliver glory days.

Ronaldo's Portugal era is the most successful era in the country's history.

The Euro 2016 triumph - Portugal's only major tournament win - and the two Nations League titles were moments when he stood in the middle of a nation's celebration, even if injury had forced him to watch the majority of that European Championship final from the sidelines, coaching and cajoling his team-mates with his leg strapped.

The face-off with Zlatan Ibrahimovic in the 2014 World Cup play-off was an epic showdown - and emphatically won by Ronaldo hitting a hat-trick in the second leg to Ibrahimovic's two goals to send Portugal to Russia at Sweden's expense.

"I know Portugal needed me in these matches and I showed that I am here," he said afterwards. And he was almost always there, across six World Cups and six European Championships. Ronaldo matched Pauleta's Portugal scoring record of 47 in 2014 - and then obliterated it, with his final tally at 146.

"I spent my life working to become the best player in the world," Ronaldo said in his international retirement statement. "Today, I realise that my greatest victory was earning the honour of representing the best country in the world."

They are fond words from a man who captained Portugal 172 times. England supporters who remember the 2006 World Cup and Ronaldo's part in the red card for his Manchester United team-mate Wayne Rooney will know how much the national jersey meant to him. The infamous wink underlined where his strongest allegiance lay.

But that meant that Ronaldo, always full of emotion, seemed to feel the blows of international defeat even more emphatically than with his clubs. And, inevitably, across that vast period of time, there were crushing lows.

The image of him breaking down as he exited the 2022 World Cup through the tunnel cruelly captured the pain of falling short on the biggest of stages.

The intensity of focus and pressure on him to deliver in those moments was immense.

"There were also moments when I couldn't give the Portuguese people what they so desperately wanted," he conceded in his statement on Thursday. "Defeats that still hurt to remember."

A shock loss to Greece in the final of Euro 2004 on home soil in his first tournament playing for his country was an early warning it would not be straightforward. Neither was replicating his prolific club scoring form in the crunch moments.

Ronaldo scored just once in four separate World Cups and his first and only World Cup knockout goal didn't come until this summer, a penalty against Croatia. Did that cost a talented Portugal generation more silverware?

Messi was targeted with similar criticism through the majority of his Argentina career. But that narrative was smashed in recent years. The 2022 World Cup win, two Copa America titles, and a run to another World Cup final this year meant Messi's international career finished at the very top.

Ronaldo's finished with him an unused substitute in Norway, after a summer in which it often seemed his presence in the Portugal XI was to the detriment of the team. At the age of 41, Ronaldo was unable to justify the system still being set up to serve him.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Goncalo Ramos scored the winner against Croatia in injury-time, after Ronaldo had been subbed off. He'd also scored a hat-trick in a 6-1 demolition of Switzerland at the previous World Cup, when Ronaldo had fallen out with coach Fernando Santos and been dropped for the last-16 tie.

Ramos was there scoring the winner in Norway, too, as Ronaldo warmed up, bristling about what he would call broken promises and a breach of trust from Portugal boss Jorge Jesus. He left that last camp early and it was an ugly exit.

Ronaldo's subsequent reveal of the eight points he wanted Jesus to make in an apologetic press conference - including reference to himself as "someone of the stature of Pele or Maradona" - reflected the self-confidence, arrogance and self-centred focus which had propelled him to the very top of the game. But also meant he would never slip down into the role of a squad player.

Such is Ronaldo's enormous profile, his very presence at this summer's World Cup seemed essential to the industry. A red-card ban he'd received against the Republic of Ireland was helpfully cancelled by FIFA, allowing Ronaldo to feature from the first whistle in North America. Portugal's exit to Spain in the last-16 was an anti-climax.

Ronaldo has blown the final whistle now, himself. The Portuguese FA, which gave out the mildest of punishments for his September outburst and walkout, have promised a big send-off. Will there be extra-time? Another runout? Don't bet against it.

Whether Portugal do actually go on to thrive as a more cohesive unit without Ronaldo also remains to be seen. But his was an extraordinary international career which will be etched into history, with his individual records in a Portugal shirt towering high.

#738. Bournemouth’s decision not to panic after their tough start is paying off

Marco Rose’s team did not win any of their first six games in the Premier League but he stayed calm and positive

It would have been easy, understandable even, for Bournemouth fans to feel down and worried. Their revered head coach, Andoni Iraola, had left in the summer and his replacement, Marco Rose, had not got off to a great start. Three defeats and three draws was all they had to show from their first six league matches, and whispers about Rose’s future had begun in the media.

But Bournemouth fans know it can take a while for new ideas and methods to yield positive results. Iraola didn’t win any of his first nine Premier League games in charge of the club and he ended up having a remarkable impact.

Still, the outlook wasn’t great after Bournemouth were hammered 5-1 by Chelsea. But Rose maintained his level-headedness. He had been adamant until that point that Bournemouth’s performances had been better than results suggested. “It’s about results at this level. But performance-wise, I see a lot of good things,” he said.

Rose was much less understanding after the hammering at Stamford Bridge, but again there were still reasons to think the result was harsh. Chelsea’s five goals came from only 1.1 expected goals (xG). The standard of their finishing was incredibly high at times, with Jordan Henderson scoring twice from outside the box (one a free-kick) and João Pedro rifling emphatically into the roof of the net from a Pedro Neto cut-back. And Morgan Rogers’ effort was helped by a deflection. Bournemouth created opportunities, with a greater xG total (1.38) than their hosts, but ended up on the end of a hiding.

The one-sided result was something of a novelty, but the overriding sense that Bournemouth had been unlucky was familiar. Not much had gone their way in the five matches before that. In their defeat at Manchester City on the opening weekend, Bournemouth led 1-0 until the 84th minute, before losing 2-1.

In their second match of the season, they were denied by a 90th-minute equaliser in a 1-1 draw with Everton. “As a coach, you evaluate the performance as well as the result, and in most phases of the game it was really good,” Rose said. “I don’t want to blame anyone because I saw so many positive things.” Next up, an 88th-minute leveller rescued Newcastle a 2-2 draw from 2-0 down at St James’ Park. And in their fourth match of the season, Bournemouth led twice against Brentford but had to settle for a 2-2 draw after individual errors from Adrien Truffert and Djordje Petrovic.

Rose continued to focus on the positives. There was an acceptance that results needed to catch up eventually, though he liked a lot of what he was watching. “I’m really happy with the confidence the lads came here today to take the three points,” he said after the Newcastle draw. Even after the loss to Liverpool left them with only three points from a possible 15, Rose cut an optimistic figure, saying: “We played a good game against Liverpool. They had some days more to recover, and I think we looked fit, even at the end. We were the team that went for a goal.”

Bournemouth won the “xG battle” four times in their first six matches. That obviously doesn’t count for much in real terms, but it shows that they were creating more high-value opportunities than their opponents. Their position of 18th in the table was not a clear reflection of their performances. “We can see the table. Now it’s up to us to prove we can handle the situation,” Rose challenged his players after the Chelsea loss.

We can use expected points (xPts) to support the idea that Bournemouth’s position was false. Our xPts model uses xG data from each match to calculate how games “deserved” to finish based on the quality and quantity of chances at each end. Although Bournemouth were in the relegation zone with three points, their 8.4 xPts put them comfortably in mid-table.

Rose’s optimistic appraisals should not be overlooked as standard post-match managerial guff either. There’s an argument his positivity and clarity played a big role in helping the Bournemouth players appreciate they were on the right track even when results were underwhelming. The worry was the team could lose confidence and sink, but hindsight suggests the coach did well to mitigate such a threat.

Since the defeat to Chelsea, Bournemouth have played six and won six in all competitions. They have scored 16 goals from 16.4 xG and allowed their opponents chances worth only 0.81 xG on average – and, crucially, Henderson’s free-kick at Stamford Bridge was the last goal they conceded. They have beaten Sturm Graz and Milan in the Europa League, Aston Villa in the League Cup, and Sunderland, Manchester United and Leeds in the Premier League.

Their recent fixtures have been slightly kinder given they played City, Newcastle, Liverpool and Chelsea – three of which were away – during their first six Premier League outings. But Milan and Leeds both made decent starts to the season, Villa have been resurgent of late, and wins at Old Trafford can never be taken for granted.

The outlook for Bournemouth is now considerably different in the Premier League. Those three wins have lifted them to eighth in the table, and because their recent victories have been so comprehensive, they’ve absolutely shot up the xPts table as well. Only Arsenal (18.2), Man City (17.1) and Nottingham Forest (15.5) can better Bournemouth’s 15.4 xPts over the full season to date.

It’s been an impressive transformation but Rose isn’t trying to take the credit. “I would love to say I’m a magician and I changed some good stuff, but sometimes it’s just about getting this kind of experience, and then if you react well that’s always the most important thing,” he mused before the Leeds win. “You can make mistakes – you can lose, you can have a bad day – but the reaction is the most important thing, and I think we showed a good reaction. We didn’t lack much, and now we just have the last ​5​% in everything.”

Evanilson finding some form in front of goal has helped, with the Brazilian scoring in each of his past four league outings, his four goals coming from 2.8 xG. Bournemouth have also limited their opposition’s flow of high-quality chances. And their upcoming fixture list looks kind.

Over the next five matches, only Coventry and Aston Villa have more straightforward schedules than Bournemouth according to our rankings. Their climb could yet continue.

Bournemouth’s surge up the table shows how quickly a club’s fortunes can change, and it’s evidence of how patience can be rewarded when it might be easier to panic. Rose may not feel as though he has changed much, but ensuring his team retained belief when heads might have dropped is as valuable as any tactical alteration.

Assessing the prospect of becoming a two-weight world champion, Baumgardner said: "It would just build the résumé. With women's boxing, we have to look at who people are fighting and the reasoning.

#735. AI agents run this automated biology lab that sequences DNA and more

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Heidi Ledford reports for Nature from Seattle, Washington.

A self-driving lab named AutoDNA can work out the constituent ‘letters’ in a snippet of DNA.Credit: Turtle Rock Scientific/Science Source/Science Photo Library

To say that someone has ‘good hands’ is high praise in a molecular biology laboratory, where researchers must deftly handle delicate glassware, pipette samples and more. But in an unusual genetics lab at Shanghai Jiao Tong University in China, a team of robots driven by artificial intelligence is designing and doing experiments with no hands to speak of.

The facility, described today1 in Nature, is one of the latest steps towards ‘self-driving’ labs that are guided by AI, with minimal input from human scientists. With samples moved around by robotic arms, the Shanghai lab can operate more than 20 types of instrument, complete thousands of operations in a single project and do experiments that involve synthesizing and sequencing DNA, among other tasks.

An experiment is designed and executed from start to finish by a team of AI agents, following a simple prompt from a human operator. After that, human hands are needed only to refresh reagents and to service hardware.

The system, called AutoDNA, is remarkable both for its degree of autonomy and because it can readily incorporate a diverse range of lab equipment, says Milad Abolhasani, a chemical engineer at North Carolina State University in Raleigh. “The future of science is going to involve a lot of autonomous labs.”

Labs have long incorporated automation into their workflows, using machines to conduct specific aspects of experimental protocols, such as mixing and heating chemicals. Now, some researchers are hoping to harness increasingly sophisticated AI tools to create self-driving labs, in which an AI system designs and executes complex experiments, troubleshoots and tweaks protocols, and orchestrates activities across an entire lab that is chock-full of disparate equipment.

Designing such labs for molecular biology is challenging because of the field’s complex workflows, which require assorted equipment and high precision, says Haibo Chen, a computer scientist at Shanghai Jiao Tong University and a co-author of the report. “In many existing systems, human experts are still required to configure the instruments,” he says. “AI is mostly added to handle just one part of the process.”

To create a more fully autonomous lab, Chen and his colleagues decided to construct it from the start with AI in mind, rather than adding AI capabilities to a pre-existing system.

The team tested AutoDNA by tasking it with a variety of projects, including detecting a cancer-linked mutation in a sample of DNA. In another experiment, the researchers asked the system to encode a message in DNA using its four nucleotide bases, abbreviated as A, C, G and T. They selected a popular quote, often misattributed to cosmologist Stephen Hawking: “Intelligence is the ability to adapt to change.”

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03552-8

Read the related News & Views, ‘AI agents enter the ‘wet lab’’.

In his report the referee, Fernando Patrick Drosghic Modesto, said the trouble began early in the second half, ⁠when a number of Uberlandia officials invaded the field after one of their players was sent off.

#733. Uefa faces political flashpoint over Sevastopol’s ascent in Russian football

Promotion to third tier for Crimean club would be clear violation of governing body’s rules amid conflict in Ukraine

Uefa and Fifa face a decisive test of their appetite to punish Russia’s integration of teams from illegally occupied Ukrainian territory after FC Sevastopol, from Crimea, won promotion to the country’s professional third tier.

Sevastopol were declared champions of group one in Football National League (FNL) 2B, in effect Russia’s fourth division, last month and are believed to have applied for a licence to compete at the level above. Should it be granted and they proceed to FNL 2A, it would appear a violation of Uefa rules that prohibit Crimean clubs from playing in competitions organised by the Russian Football Union (RFU). The governing body would come under severe pressure to extend sanctions on European football’s pariah state, whose club and national teams are banned from competing in international tournaments.

“Of course, we plan to submit documents,” the Sevastopol CEO Valery Chaly told local media last month. “According to the regulations we should advance to the next stage.” The RFU remains a member of Uefa and Fifa but there would be fresh calls for it to be ejected if Sevastopol’s ascent is not blocked. It is understood no decision about their potential admission has been made.

Football’s governing bodies were given a similar dilemma in 2023 when Sevastopol and another Crimean club, Rubin Yalta, were accepted into FNL 2B even though sides from the occupied territory have not been allowed to compete in Russia since its annexation in 2014.

The Ukrainian Association of Football (UAF) asked Uefa and Fifa to consider ejecting Russia, alleging a “gross violation” of their statutes and Uefa’s ruling, made in 2014, that Crimean clubs must not compete in RFU-run events. Uefa claimed it would assess the situation but the authorities appeared to turn a blind eye, the RFU saying it had created a workaround by making FNL 2B an amateur competition that it did not operate. At the time, several clubs at that level contacted by the Guardian confirmed informally that they were fully professional. No such blurring of the lines exists for FNL 2A, which has never denied its clubs are professional.

That unwillingness to act led to escalation when, in April 2024, an imitation of the Ukrainian club Zorya Luhansk – whose home city in Donbas is illegally occupied by Russia – was admitted to FNL 2B. This year they were joined by a fake Shakhtar Donetsk, mimicking the current Champions League side who have been forced to play elsewhere since 2014. Five of the 15 teams who completed the recent FNL 2B group one season played in or claimed to represent occupied areas, the Simferopol-based club Kyzyltash Bakhchisaray completing the quintet.

Should the RFS decide, of its own accord or under pressure from international bodies, to bar Sevastopol from promotion an even bigger flashpoint may await. The imitation Shakhtar finished runners-up in group 1, securing that spot by winning 2-0 at Sevastopol on the season’s final day last Saturday, and are next in line to go up. Unlike Sevastopol their home matches are played on Russian territory, in Taganrog, rather than an occupied area. The club is, however, registered to an address in Donetsk.

In October 2025 the UAF asked Uefa to review and explain the imitation clubs’ legal positions but, as with any assessment of the Crimean clubs’ participation, the results are still awaited. It warned of a“coordinated political attempt to legitimise the occupation and erase the identity of Ukrainian football”.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Last month Russia competed in a Fifa-run event for the first time since the invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, finishing 19th in the new under-15 World Cup. Teams at under-15 and under-16 levels have continued to play in smaller Uefa development tournaments, largely against invited opponents on home soil, during the war in Ukraine.

None of Uefa, Fifa, the RFU, the FNL, Sevastopol or the imitation Shakhtar Donetsk offered comment when contacted by the Guardian.

#731. Many Turkish 'guest workers' hit by poverty in old age

West Germany and Turkey signed an agreement allowing the temporary recruitment of workers on October 30, 1961. Sixty-five years on, many so-called 'guest workers' can't live from their pensions.

Düsseldorf Airport is a historically symbolic location. This is where the first Turkish "guest workers," as they were called at the time in Germany, arrived 65 years ago.

At a ceremony there in in mid-September, North Rhine-Westphalia's premier, Henrik Wüst, commemorated the courage of this first generation of migrants and their contribution to Germany's prosperity.

By the time recruitment ended in 1973, some 870,000 Turkish men and women had migrated to Germany for work. They toiled in the coal mines, did piecework on assembly lines or cleaned factory floors. Most settled in Düsseldorf, Cologne or Duisburg. "They have made our country more diverse, more open and stronger," said Wüst. However, he also stressed: "We will have reached our goal only once name, skin color and religion no longer matter."

According to integration expert Haci-Halil Uslucan, Germany is still a long way from that.

Even 65 years later, he told DW, people of Turkish descent still suffer a great deal of discrimination in Germany.

But he believes that the German Turkish labor recruitment agreement was, in the main, a success story.

"We've seen success in many areas, such as education. Today, we have a large number of college graduates, and we've seen professional advancement. And successful political careers. Take Baden-Württemberg's state premier, Cem Özdemir, for example," he said.

Uslucan himself is one such a success story. His father came to Berlin from Turkey and worked in the textile industry. Two years later, his father brought his wife and two sons to join him in Germany.

Haci-Halil Uslucan subsequently earned his Ph.D. in psychology and a professor of contemporary Turkish studies at the University of Duiburg-Essen.

One of his most recent research topics addresses the dark side of the labor recruitment agreement. He is examining loneliness, an issue that affects and troubles many former so-called "guest workers."

But poverty is also increasingly taking its toll on some people of Turkish descent reaching retirement age.

With a rate of between 25-30%, poverty in old age is twice as high among migrants in Germany than among Germans, which is about 12-14%, he says, adding that the disability rate and the rate of early retirement are significantly higher among migrants because the first generation did very heavy physical labor.

They are also twice as likely to become unemployed 10 years before reaching retirement age, says Uslucan.

"In addition, their monthly income is lower, they are more likely to have had employment gaps and worked in low-wage sectors. As a result, their pensions are also low."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

An analysis by Germany's pension insurance fund (DRV) for the Mediendienst Integration, an information service for journalists on migration topics, uncovered some alarming figures: In Germany, pensioners with Turkish citizenship receive, on average, about €890 ($997) in pension benefits per month. That is €360 less than German pensioners, who receive €1,250 per month on average.

Even more troubling is that in June 2026, more than three times as many retirees with Turkish citizenship relied on top-up welfare benefits as Germans (9.3% compared to 2.7%).

One reason for this is that many of the Turkish workers who came to Germany were already in the middle of their working lives and consequently has less years to contribute to their pension fund, social scientist Eric Seils of the Hans Böckler Foundation in Düsseldorf told DW.

"But, of course, the most important reason is that they earned less in wages and had a shorter work history. The guest workers who came to Germany often went straight to factories, mines or construction sites. There, they didn't earn high hourly wages because they were often less educated than the Germans," he added.

With deindustrialization in the early 1970s and the oil crisis, many Turkish workers in Germany also lost their jobs.

"There weren't as many good jobs available at traditional industrial companies. Those who weren't as well-educated were more likely to become unemployed than those with an education — and the same was true for Germans. And when working lives are interrupted, that naturally has an impact on retirement benefits at some point."

Janina Söhn of the Institute for Sociological Research (SOFI) at Göttingen University has also studied the issue of poverty among older immigrants in Germany.

It's a major problem in Germany that nearly one-third of immigrants are at risk of poverty, she said.

"This group faces even greater hardship than, for example, women in general, who already have a higher risk of poverty. And when you then look specifically at female migrants living alone, the figures are truly dire and alarming. If there were no family support, it would be an even sorrier situation."

Older Turkish migrants in Germany also often have limited opportunities to earn extra euros during retirement.

This is because either because they are poorly qualified or because the hard physical labor they performed when they were younger has left them physically unfit.

According to figures from Germany's Federal Employment Agency, the employment rate of for retired Turkish people living in Germany is only half that of Germans (5.2% compared to 10.8%).

"Basically, they face a whole series of disadvantages or hardships in life. That generation of guest workers was brought to Germany and then had to do the worst jobs here, whereas many Germans were able to progress through education and training," Söhn said.

The Turkish workers in Germany didn't get similar chances.

"The people who did these tough jobs, which are always necessary for any economy, paid for it with their health," she said.

This article was originally written in German.

#729. Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane signs new contract with Bayern through to 2029

‘I love the club, fans and the city of Munich,’ says striker

Kane has 156 goals in 161 Bayern games since 2023

England captain and Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane has signed a new deal with Bayern Munich through to 2029, the German club have announced.

Kane moved to Bayern from Tottenham in 2023 for a record €100m fee and has proved a huge success, scoring 156 goals in 161 competitive appearances and leading the German club to two Bundesliga titles and a DFB Cup.

The 33-year-old was named as the world’s best male player last week after scoring a remarkable 89 goals for club and country since the start of August 2025, becoming the first Englishman to win the Ballon d’Or in 25 years and the first Bayern player since Karl-Heinz Rummenigge in 1981 to win the award.

“I feel right at home at FC Bayern,” said Kane. “I love the club, the fans and the city of Munich. We have a fantastic team and, in Vincent Kompany, a fantastic manager. It makes me very proud to be part of this club. My whole family is very happy here. I was keen to stay. I’m now looking forward to the future and I want to win many more titles with this great club.”

In September, Kane became the fastest player in German history to reach 100 Bundesliga goals, doing so in 98 games to shatter the previous record set by Dieter Mueller in 1977 by 31 games.

Bayern did not disclose ⁠financial details of the agreement. However, German media reported that the extension is ​the most lucrative contract ​in the club’s history and part ​of a long-term commitment to the England captain.

“We’re absolutely delighted, because with Harry Kane we have the Ballon d’Or winner on the pitch – a team player, a leader, the best all-round striker in the world,” said Christoph Freund, Bayern’s sporting director. “We all benefit from his qualities as a player and as a person, day in, day out. FC Bayern thrives on players who never stop giving their all, even when they have already achieved the greatest of goals.”

This month Kane equalled England’s all-time men’s caps record, while nudging his international goal tally to 91 in 125 appearances.

For more facts about Wheel of Fortune, keep reading…

1. Created by Merv Griffin, Wheel of Fortune debuted as a daytime game show on NBC in 1975 and was based on the word game “Hangman.” 2. Pat Sajak took on the role of host in 1981, and Vanna White joined the show as cohost the following year. In 1983, Wheel of Fortune went into syndication. Its spinoff Celebrity Wheel of Fortune debuted on ABC in 2021.3. Born in Chicago, Pat started his career in the broadcasting industry. According to his bio, he joined the United States Army in 1968 and was part of Armed Forces Radio in Saigon during his time in Vietnam. Afterwards, Pat continued to work at radio and TV stations, where he fulfilled the roles of staff announcer, talk show host and weatherman. In fact, he was working as a star weatherman in Los Angeles when he received a call from Merv asking if he’d like to host Wheel of Fortune. “I swear, the first thought was, 'There’s nothing for me to do,’” Pat recalled to daughter and Wheel of Fortune social correspondent Maggie Sajak in a June 2024 video. “I mean, 'Yes, there are three R’s' is not exactly a career mover….Shows you what I know.”

4. As for Vanna, she grew up in South Carolina. According to her bio, she studied at a fashion design school in Atlanta before pursuing a career in modeling—with her then moving to L.A. to try acting. It was there she was spotted by Merv and auditioned for Wheel of Fortune. “I was probably more nervous than any other person that auditioned,” Vanna told CBS 58 in 2019, “and 200 girls auditioned—and I was the last one.” 5. In fact, Wheel of Fortune previously revealed that the very first letter Vanna turned on the puzzle board was T.6. Meanwhile, Jim Thornton joined Wheel of Fortune as the announcer in 2011. Previously, he did voice work for several movies, TV shows and commercials—including Monsters, Inc., Rugrats and Celebrity Deathmatch.

7. Before Pat retired in June 2024, he and Vanna had appeared on more than 8,000 episodes of Wheel of Fortune across 41 seasons of syndication. 8. He actually secured a Guinness World Records title in 2019 for longest career as a game show host on the same show. 9. Vanna has broken records, too. In 2013, she was presented with the “most frequent clapper” title—with Guinness World Records estimating she clapped at least 3,480,864 times across 30 seasons. If you break it down and factor in her rare absences, that comes out to about 606 claps per show, according to the organization.

10. Wheel of Fortune attracts more than 20 million viewers every week, per a 2023 press release. 11. But let’s talk about the prizes. According to the show’s 2024 numbers, it awarded nearly 600 cars to contestants in 41 seasons. 12. Not to mention it had given away nearly 5,000 vacations by that point. 13. And if you’re wondering how much money Wheel of Fortune has distributed, the show said at the time it’s handed out more than $324 million in cash and prizes.

14. Vanna has also racked up a lot of steps walking across the puzzle board—the equivalent of two marathons (about 52 miles!), per the show’s figures. 15. As for her dazzling dresses, Vanna’s worn more than 7,000. But, no, she doesn’t get to keep them.16. And, amazingly, Vanna didn’t have an outfit repeat for nearly four decades. “Can you believe for the first time ever I wore the same dress twice after 7,000 dresses?” she told social media followers in a September 2020 video while holding up a blue frock. “Ugh! This is so 2020.”

17. Of course, it wouldn’t be Wheel of Fortune without the wheel. It’s a big one, too—weighing 2,400 pounds per ABC News. 18. And it’s one-of-a-kind. The outlet reported the show brings the wheel to all its destinations by breaking it down and then reconstructing it—with the program typically traveling with more than a million pounds of equipment. 19. Plus, ABC News states the Bonus Wheel has more than 24 envelopes filled with prizes.

20. If you’re puzzled by how the show works, allow Vanna to explain. When it comes to filming, she told WLKY in 2015, “We only do four days, but six shows each day.” 21. As for the puzzle board, Wheel of Fortune got a new one in 2022 that’s one giant screen. “This year, we switched to a laser,” Vanna explained in a YouTube video at the time. “I don’t even have to touch it. I just stick my hand by it.” 22. And while prices may fluctuate over time, the show shared the cost to buy a vowel has stayed at $250 throughout the past four decades.23. Ever wonder how Pat knows the exact number of letters in a puzzle so quickly after a contestant guesses? He’d like to solve this one. As he explained in a 2021 YouTube video, the behind-the-scenes team would listen to ensure the right letter is called and then relay the correct number to Pat through a TV screen that he could see from his hosting spot on the set.

24. There’s also a used letter board the contestants can view to help them keep track of which consonants and vowels have already been called. “You never see that at home, but our players see it,” Pat said in the same video. “So every time a letter is called that letter comes off, that light turns off, and they know not to call it again—except when they do call it again….I kid our players, but, believe me, I understand the pressures they’re under.” 25. If you love the Toss Up puzzles, you can thank Pat for those. As he explained, Wheel of Fortune was facing a challenge: “How do we get more content and not take up a lot of time?” Pat told Maggie. “So I did come up with the Toss Up puzzles, and they’ve worked real well. And then our producer added the Triple Toss Up. And then I added the idea of $10,000 if you get all three because it’s not my money, what do I care?”26. In January 2015, reporter Christopher Ingraham published an analysis for The Washington Post that looked at 1,546 final bonus puzzles from 2007 to that year. Based on his examination, he wrote that H, G, P and O were the letters most likely to appear in these puzzles at the time (taking into account that contestants are already given the letters R, S, T, L, N and E). However, Ingraham found that players chose these letters less frequently than they selected C, D, M and A—even though, according to his analysis, the latter set of letters appeared less frequently back then.

#727. Japan FA’s Kozo Tashima to stand against Infantino for Fifa presidency

Tashima says he brings ‘honest, sound, upright attitude’

He is understood to have acted with the blessing of Uefa

The Japan Football Association’s honorary president, Kozo Tashima, ⁠has announced his intention to stand against Gianni Infantino in March’s Fifa presidential election.

Tashima is the second challenger to declare in advance of the 18 November deadline after the former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega, although it remains unclear whether Vega has the backing of five of Fifa’s 211 member associations, which is required to take a place on the ballot in Rabat.

The widely respected Tashima will have no problem in securing the nominations and is understood to have acted with the blessing of Uefa, which has led the opposition to Infantino after his failed attempt to sell off a 20% stake in Fifa’s commercial rights this summer.

In the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.

If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.

If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from the iOS App Store on iPhone or the Google Play store on Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.

The former Japan international has many allies in Europe and had talks with Uefa officials at last month’s Asian Football Confederation (AFC) congress in Tokyo.

“I am grateful that I can make this announcement with the full support of the Japan Football Association,” Tashima told the Japanese newspaper Sports Nippon. “It’s not about winning or losing but about conveying to the world the honest, sound and upright attitude that Japanese football has built. What Fifa ⁠needs now are these values that we have protected. I have decided to run in order ‌to make this appeal to the world.”

The declaration is an intriguing development after the AFC congress concluded with its president, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim al-Khalifa, publicly endorsing Infantino in a major U-turn, having previously sided with Uefa and Concacaf – the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation – in attempting to depose him.

Tashima could split the AFC vote and is certain to pick up votes from Europe and Concacaf, although other candidates could emerge.

Uefa has spent months attempting to find a candidate to stand against Infantino, but may have concluded that a non-European challenger will fare better owing to widespread resentment about its perceived dominance of the sport.

#725. Fifa wants to restrict women’s Olympic football to under-23s in controversial move

IOC open to dialogue and Fifa wants input from others

Fifa concerned about fixture congestion and workload

Fifa wants the International Olympic Committee to restrict the women’s Olympic football tournament to under-23s owing to concerns over fixture congestion and the workload of senior players.

The eligibility criteria for the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles has been set, with qualification tournaments having begun in some regions, so no change can be made until Brisbane 2032 at the earliest, but sources at both organisations have told the Guardian that they are open to dialogue.

Although no formal proposal has been made, Fifa is understood to be interested in examining the matter in talks with the IOC and other key stakeholders, such as the players and leading member associations whose national sides routinely qualify for the Games.

A move to bring in age restrictions would dramatically alter the nature of the event and require careful analysis, consultation and consideration through Fifa and IOC processes.

Such a change would be controversial and could provoke a backlash from leading international players because the Olympics has long been regarded as one of the highlights of the women’s calendar, with Emma Hayes’s United States team securing gold in Paris two years ago. The Olympic title has been contested eight times and the US have won five.

Women’s football also has a major commercial appeal for the IOC, particularly in markets such as the US, Europe and Australia, so it may resist Fifa’s overtures.

Women’s football was introduced to the Olympics at Atlanta in 1996, and as an amateur sport at that time never had eligibility requirements, in contrast to the men’s game.

After admitting football to the Olympic programme in 1908 the IOC did not permit professionals to take part until 1984 owing to Fifa’s insistence on maintaining the primacy of the World Cup, as well as the demands on players from a congested calendar. Under pressure from Fifa the IOC introduced an under-23 age restriction in 1992, although three overage players have also been allowed in each squad since 1996.

The huge growth and professionalisation of the women’s game over the past decade has created increased fixture congestion, with the 2028 calendar the most bloated yet.

Fifa is to a large extent culpable for this because the world governing body has chosen to launch the Women’s Club World Cup in an Olympic year, with the US to stage the 16-team competition between 5 and 30 January, six months before the Games.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

The Women’s Club World Cup will cause major disruption to the European club season, with Arsenal and Chelsea or Manchester City likely to be absent from domestic competition for up to a month if they reach the latter stages, missing four Women’s Super League matches and the FA Cup fourth round.

The importance of the sport to the IOC is shown by the fact that the women’s football tournament will be bigger than the men’s for the first time in LA, featuring 16 teams to 12 in a reversal of the numbers at Paris 2024.

43 players and eight members of staff received red cards after the brawl, as well as two board members

A world record of 53 red cards were shown during a chaotic under-20s game in Brazil.

The semi-final first leg of the Minas Gerais Under-20 Championship tie between Uberlandia and Mamore was marred by scenes that led to 43 players and eight members of coaching staff being sent off.

The previous record was 36, in a 2011 fifth-division game between Club Atletico Claypole and Victoriano Arenas in Argentina.

Brazilian news outlet O Tempo reported the military police were called, external because of extensive damage to the Parque do Sabia Stadium.

According to the referee's report, a brawl broke out in the second half after Mamores' Davi taunted the opposition bench during celebrations when his side went 3-1 up.

Uberlandia goalkeeping coach Paulo Sergio Dias Dos Santos ran on to the pitch to confront him, sparking clashes and the subsequent dismissals, with three players having already been sent off earlier.

The police report referenced 14 broken doors, damaged shower facilities, broken windows and that benches, tables and chairs had been destroyed.

The game was paused for approximately 40 minutes and then abandoned by referee Fernando Patrick Drosghic Modesto.

"In the 54th minute of the second âhalf, a generalized brawl broke out, making it impossible to show the red cards and to carry âout the â match-closing protocol," Modesto wrote in his report.

"Therefore, owing to all the turmoil and the lack of security, I declared the match ended."

Uberlandia have since confirmed, external that they have conceded the second leg of the semi-final because Mamore only have seven players available as a result of all the red cards.

They described their move as a "gesture of fair play" as Mamore would progress through to the final, and Uberlandia will instead focus on the third-place match.

"The club has also not remained silent: âthe appropriate disciplinary measures regarding those involved have already been taken internally, because athletic development is, above all, a âmatter of personal development," Uberlandia added.

#721. The international break is almost here: so wave goodbye to your players, and maybe your manager | Max Rushden

What used to be a time to reset is now a time to rehire, and Michael Carrick is not the only Premier League manager looking over his shoulder

Perhaps the most telling moment of Manchester United’s comeback against Roma was at the final whistle. The camera focused on Michael Carrick, who shook the hand of Gian Piero Gasperini before looking around trying to remember what you’re meant to do after a victory. The camera then cut to the director of football, Jason Wilcox, and chief executive, Omar Berrada, clapping with two of the most ashen faces you could imagine – as if it was a minute’s applause in the 87th minute for a lifelong octogenarian fan who died peacefully in his sleep earlier in the week (most probably not at a United game but you couldn’t rule it out).

Of course there are rules about smiling when you are involved with a failing football club. Players can’t be seen to be enjoying themselves in the week after a defeat, managers have to be earnest at almost all times, apart from when a journalist’s phone goes off at a press conference – a moment of sporting hilarity on a par with a pigeon landing on Centre Court.

So it stands to reason that Wilcox and Berrada were right not to be shirtless, swirling their Ineos gilets around their heads at full time. Same goes for the other one, also known as head of recruitment Christopher Vivell, who has borrowed Rodri’s cloak of invisibility for this whole saga. Of all the free passes going in the game at the moment, he is playing a blinder.

But were they so solemn because they’d just agreed terms with Unai Emery at half-time (don’t sue me, Nassef – that was clumsy, wrong and tongue-in-cheek, keep on keeping on, keep on ascending, lots of love xoxoxox)? You couldn’t blame them. And 45 minutes later United are BACK. It was an astonishing turnaround. Where has that front-foot, aggressive football been?

There was quite a lot of luck - a soft penalty missed and retaken, a wild miskick, Roma missing a hatful of chances before the break. All those moments could have signalled the end.

It is unlikely that the penalty is Carrick’s Mark Robins/Adrian Heath moment, but win at home against Aston Villa on Sunday and it is not beyond the realms of possibility that he turns the season around. It is also not beyond the realms of possibility that United are so badly run that they get a lucky win over Villa, stick with Carrick and revert to what we’ve seen and end up surviving Spurs-style on the last day.

You will have heard every pundit mention the hierarchy waiting for the international break to make the call. Perhaps Sim Jim Ratcliffe saw how much content Manchester City gave us in the previous one and wants the column inches.

But it isn’t only Carrick who will be sweating while watching a repeat of Pointless Celebrities or whatever else is in place of Match Of the Day when the Premier League has a week off. There are realistically five managers who may not be in place when we all return.

From the bottom up: Régis Le Bris at Sunderland, who host good-at-attacking-bad-at-defending Chelsea on Sunday. This would be a classic case of victim of your own success. Qualify for Europe for the first time in more than 50 years, fail to recruit adequately, then chuck out the manager who achieved that success. But if Bromley can get rid of Andy Woodman, anything is possible.

If you want evidence all is not well at the Stadium of Light, a friend recently took a posh taxi in Yarm that had No 34 embroidered into all the seats, plus three screens and the night sky on the ceiling. If Granit Xhaka is selling his personalised Renault Espace, perhaps Le Bris has lost the dressing room. Either that or Granit’s just embroidered a Hummer. Look I don’t have many sources, so I can only work with what I’ve got.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

In 19th position: Oliver Glasner and Nottingham Forest. A tricky home game with Manchester City* late on Saturday afternoon. His “too many compromises” comments reminded me of a baffling perfume advert from the 2010s where a man announces at a press conference that he’s no longer going to be the man he’s expected to be any more, ignoring the fact none of us know what he was expected to be in the first place. Was Glasner talking about the players or the looming presence in the directors’ box? Is Evangelos Marinakis insisting on taking the rondos? Or has Glasner spent the past three months telling Liam Delap to try to take a bit off it and opt for placement, with Delap resolute in using every bit of his “shot power – 99” at every opportunity?

In 18th: Pierre Sage at Crystal Palace. He doesn’t have a lot going for him. I can’t speak for everyone, but let me try. No one watched how good Lens were last season under Sage and they appear worse now if shipping 9 (nine) at home to Como is anything to go by. So Sage appearing unknown and dour leads to all manner of pundits announcing how uninspiring he is. Perhaps he’s a hoot at training. Palace have sold a lot of good players and replaced them with not as good players, which feels like a risk. Yet you fear for him, you really do.

And then there’s Matthias Jaissle at Newcastle. Could defeat at Fulham spell the end for him? The common theme appears to be selling the spine of a team and expecting a new guy to deliver. And yet there is a disconnect between him and the fans. We call for managers to be given time, but what if you give time to the wrong guy? Jaissle has a good reputation but even Geordies still completely invested in the PIF project probably didn’t watch too many of his Al-Ahli games over the past three years.

So we are left with five managers on the brink, all ready for a massive payout for not doing a great job – something I’ve been attempting to get for 20 years of mid-level broadcasting, sadly to no avail. All the while Sean Dyche’s agent is cartwheeling around a golf club in the East Midlands adding zeros to his next deal. Football really is ridiculous when you step back and think about it.
